#2705. New Lex football's seniors are a 'special' blend of personalities

NEW LEXINGTON — The seniors on New Lexington's football team are unique, diverse and highly unified.

They grew up learning the game as little guys, enjoying success at every level before making their biggest marks in high school. They've been part of 32 wins and played in seven playoff games the past three seasons, winning a pair of Muskingum Valley League-Small School titles in the process.

They'll play in an eighth on Nov. 13 when Millersburg West Holmes makes the near-two-hour trip to Jim Rockwell Stadium for a Division IV, Region 15 semifinal. And there is no question it will be an all-for-one, one-for-all operation as it eyes another Elite Eight appearance.

Tyson Spicer wouldn't have it any other way.

"It's really crazy, just thinking that it's almost over with these guys," Spicer, the team's leading receiver, said after a recent practice. "We've literally played since the first grade. My dad (Ryan Spicer) was the head coach. We learned the no-huddle offense in first grade."

Movin' on: New Lex survives defensive showdown to shut down Heath

More: Sheridan football comeback stuns unbeaten New Lex, Week 10 roundup

All-Everything: Carter Smith 'isn't normal.' Here's why that's a good thing for West M

Who'd have known that 12 years later, before a free thinker like Kevin Board ever arrived in Perry County to coach the team, that Spicer and Co. would be running the same offense. Board's offenses have regularly been some of the MVL's best since the seniors arrived in 2022.

They have long been identified as a class with lofty potential.

"Ever since we were young, we aways knew we were going to be something special," Spicer said. "I think we have lived up to it, but we have a few more exclamation marks to put on the end of it."

Chemistry is their common ground, which is usually the case in a class with a 5-2 playoff record in three years. Even as some in the group have enjoyed more individual success than others — Spicer, lineman Eli Stephens and quarterback Lane Ratliff have been mainstays since their arrival — jealousy in the ranks has never been an issue. Nor have quarrels within the ranks.

Spicer said the bonds built through years of competition and countless hours of practice have only fortified their communication. That, he said, doesn't end when practices are completed and players go their own directions.

"I would say this is one of the most tightly knit senior classes I've seen in my life," Spicer said. "We all hang out on the weekends, go do stuff together all the time."

In his case, it also doesn't extend merely to the gridiron. Spicer is also one of the state's top wrestlers, and football classmates Dalyus Nealy and Alberto Boggess are also grappling mainstays.

"Doing both sports definitely makes you closer," Spicer said. "In wrestling, you're traveling together, staying in hotels together, cutting weight together, being miserable together. That stuff really brings you together."

There is the vocal leader in captain Tanner Toth, a veteran linebacker and receiver, who many on the team — coaches included — consider the unquestioned leader and coach on the field. The excitable personality of Terrelle King, the team leader in sacks and tackles-for-loss, lines up making splash plays opposite him.

"We have a lot of guys who lead by example, but Tanner takes that next step," Stephens said. "He's not only a great leader in how he works and what he does, but he's also a great vocal leader. That's what makes him special."

There is Spicer, the fun-loving, furry-haired big-play man. There are the newcomers, Paul Nealy and Dalyus, who moved in from Columbus as middle schoolers. Boggess, a nose man who overcame a knee injury in 2025, moved to Perry County from Florida as a biddy leaguer.

All offer their own unique blends of communication.

"For some of them, coming to a new school was different at first, but once we started playing football together, everybody meshed really well," Stephens said. "We became great friends with those guys. They may not have grown up here, but once we got into sports together everything just clocked."

Board chuckled when describing Dalyus, one of tallest cornerbacks in the state at 6-4, whose colloquial offerings can be a bit obscure.

"He's an interesting character," Board said. "Oh, how would I say it? He's the screwball personality. Some of the things he'll say are just off the wall. It's like, 'what are you saying?'"

Quarterback Lane Ratliff and Stephens are the most experienced of all and, until 2026, two of the group's most quiet.

"Lane is kind of like Eli," Spicer said. "You watch him running over everybody on the football field, but if you don't know him, I don't know if he would ever say a word to you."

"On the field, you think he's this big, intense guy," Spicer said. "But if you really get to know him, he's one of the most quiet, soft-spoken guys you'll ever talk to."

Thankfully for the Panthers, their play is quite the contrary. Both Division I recruits, Stephens is a dominant two-way committed to Army and Ratliff, a 6-foot, 200-pounder, has an offer from Charlotte.

Both played alongside elder siblings in previous years. In Stephens' case, he often followed the lead of his brother Isaiah, the team's All-Ohio quarterback in 2024.

Board said that has steadily changed with age, however, particularly within the confines of competition.

"When Isaiah was here, he was very quiet," Board said. "He just did whatever, whatever big bro said. But since he has left, (Eli) really kind of come out of his shell. He's got some good one liners."

The common denominator for the group? When the lights come on, it's all business.

"They all bring a little something different to the table," Board said. "It's a very special group. They've played a lot of games. Most of these guys played as sophomores. All of them played in last year's regional final. ... When adversity hits, they don't panic. They've been there, they've done that. Experience is the ultimate divider."

"Everybody just kind of fits together really, really well," Stephens said. "Everybody's different. But when it's time to go out there and play, everybody has the same goal, the same mentality on the football field."

#2704. NHL Power Rankings: Flyers flounder to start new season as Rick Tocchet searches for answers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2703. NFL midseason team grades include two A's and one F

The halfway point of the 2026 NFL regular season necessitates some midterm grades.

As the league enters the back half of the schedule, there's a clear sense of separation between the top contenders and the also-rans. Meanwhile, several teams have already sunk to the bottom, with seven organizations having two or fewer wins.

With nine weeks remaining, there's still a good deal of time for coaching staffs and players to reshape their fortunes. Still, the trends that emerged in the first two months of the season could be hard to shake.

Here are USA TODAY Sports' midseason grades for each team, with marks determined by how every franchise fared relative to the roster's capabilities and preseason expectations:

Kyle Shanahan's team remains the NFL's standard setter for efficiency and resilience. With injuries continuing to pile up in the receiving corps, San Francisco has still managed to get MVP-level play out of Brock Purdy while ranking first in EPA per play and second in points differential (+79). Health seems like the only thing that can truly trip the 49ers up late in the season, though a pass rush that hasn't registered a sack in the past two games will have to ramp up for Raheem Morris' unit to reach its full potential.

Amid what many saw as a potentially lost season, the Giants have found themselves. While some teams might have been sunk by losing their starting quarterback in Week 2, John Harbaugh's ingenuity paid off with the midseason acquisition and switch to J.J. McCarthy. The defense's cohesion despite the loss of Dexter Lawrence this offseason and Brian Burns to a torn anterior cruciate ligament should put coordinator Dennard Wilson on the short list for some head-coaching roles come January. Even if New York falls short of the NFC's contending class, Harbaugh has instituted some winning ways in a remarkably short window.

Under first-year coach Joe Brady, the Bills have tapped into a newfound sense of perseverance. The league's leading offense in yards per game (386.4) and scoring (32 points per game) has also set the bar for malleability, with Josh Allen able to transform the attack as needed to flatten opponents. Jim Leonhard's defense is still figuring things out on the fly, but the unit is coming up with enough game-flipping plays to sustain itself as it searches for a better sense of consistency.

After a trio of trade-deadline moves, there's no doubt that general manager James Gladstone and coach Liam Coen believe this team is a leading title contender. Should you? Maybe. At the very least, Jacksonville – which boasts the NFL's only triple-digit point differential (+108) – might be the league's most balanced team, ranking fifth offensively in EPA per play and second defensively. Trevor Lawrence looks fully in command of a system that allows him to wield any number of weapons on a given play, and defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile's opportunistic group might lessen its reliance on splash plays after its midseason acquisitions. With a fairly forgiving schedule, however, it might not be clear until the playoffs whether Jacksonville truly can make a push for the organization's first Super Bowl appearance.

With Caleb Williams coming into his own, anything feels possible for Chicago. An already sky-high ceiling was pushed even higher with the trade for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who changes the entire complexion of the unit he just joined. Williams' four interceptions in an unnecessarily close call against the Buccaneers emphasized the volatility that might be in play for this team, but the Bears look capable of leaning on their defense in key stretches rather than relying on Ben Johnson's machine-like offense not to have its gears get jammed every once in a while.

Remember when people were trying to put Matt LaFleur on the hot seat? That dramatic September start now feels like a distant memory. The offensive equilibrium is difficult to trust, with Jordan Love having to generate explosive plays at the league's highest rate in order to compensate for a last-ranked rushing attack. But as LaFleur joked last week, "Well, you guys said you wanted to let him cook, so we're letting him cook." On the other side of the ball, Jonathan Gannon has done some of the best work of any coordinator this season, harnessing the aggressiveness of a unit that should step things up another notch once Micah Parsons returns.

For most teams, the 16 consecutive wins in one-score games would be a flashing sign for a forthcoming regression. At this point, though, it's difficult to write off Denver's late-game fortitude as a matter of mere luck. The Broncos' process, which has led to the team having the league's third-worst yardage differential, certainly looks to be lacking. But if Bo Nix and the rushing attack continue to make even incremental improvements, particularly on early downs, there might not be many tougher outs in the AFC.

A secondary prone to springing massive leaks still isn't fully in the clear. Despite being dealt a bad hand on the back end, however, Dan Campbell has managed to keep Detroit squarely in the NFC North hunt. The Lions will have to continue to be innovative defensively after largely standing pat at the trade deadline, though the offense also has to pick things up a bit after hitting a midseason lull.

Kenneth Walker III has certainly done his part in rejuvenating the run game and offense at large. There's a disturbing trend in play, however, with the explosive plays that fueled the 5-0 start eroding as of late. Kansas City might have to settle for its old ways with an aerial attack that operates primarily in the underneath area for yards-after-catch opportunities, but the offense still might have more flexibility than it did in previous years. The unpredictability of the pass rush and the kicking game loom as major points of concern.

Joe Burrow has pushed his way to the forefront of the NFL MVP conversation. Dexter Lawrence has turned the defensive line into a bunch of bullies at the line of scrimmage. What's not to like about Cincinnati's trajectory? The botched Arnold Ebiketie trade didn't reflect well on the organization's attention to detail, and the fallout could have a minor effect on the pass rush that's powering the defense. Overall, though, this feels like the Bengals team that everyone has been waiting to see after a three-year playoff drought.

This hasn't been the fully dominant title follow-up that some might have expected. Still, there's plenty of reason to believe another late-season surge could be in the cards. Sam Darnold's turnovers and injuries have compounded the problems of an offense that only looks right when it's feeding Jaxon Smith-Njigba. But with Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet both finally healthy, the ground game could be poised to take off. A defense that still smothers all of its opposition increases the margin for error and gives Seattle staying power down the stretch.

Mike McCarthy might not be producing much panache in Pittsburgh, but the Steelers are prevailing thanks to an efficient ground game and revitalized defense. In a conference where few teams seem truly reliable, this is at least a fairly trustworthy group. Though it seems inevitable that better competition will exploit the troubles Aaron Rodgers and the passing attack have in dealing with the blitz and trying to work deep downfield, the Steelers can count on clean play to keep them afloat in tight matchups.

Maybe this seems like a harsh mark for a group that was the NFL's last to suffer a loss and still is in the thick of the NFC North race at 6-2. But leadership continued to embrace this specific version of a build that necessitated a cheap solution at quarterback, and it whiffed there through the first half of the season. Waking from that delusion and grabbing Kirk Cousins at the eleventh hour was a necessary step to have any hope of salvaging the season, though the 38-year-old's presence only can do so much to assist a run game that's lagging behind where it should be.

Things have looked dire at times for the defending AFC champions, who have seen Drake Maye flounder in critical spots. New England has demonstrated it can escape those valleys, but this is still an outfit that's relegated itself to the fringe of the AFC playoff picture. Given the lack of help elsewhere in the receiving corps, the Patriots probably can't afford to have A.J. Brown be out of the lineup or a non-factor for much longer.

The bottom line of a 5-4 start sure looks good for a franchise that entered the year outwardly pushing scaled-back expectations after the Myles Garrett trade. Nevertheless, it's difficult to feel as though much of Cleveland's formula – which includes the 29th-ranked scoring attack and a -32 point differential – is sustainable. Deshaun Watson continues to weigh down an offense that can't overcome his limitations, which might be inhibiting the development of the young core. And Cleveland can't seem to shake its rampant mistakes, from penalties – no team has more than the Browns' 82 – to the missed tackles dogging a defense that struggles to stop the run.

Sean McVay said he's never faced a run of personnel hits in his 10 seasons as Rams coach like he has this season – and that was before Puka Nacua landed on injured reserve. That doesn't fully absolve the preseason Super Bowl favorites for how much of a letdown this campaign has been to date, though. Los Angeles is paying for a lack of receiver depth it was long warned about, and a team that's beat up on inferior foes looks ill-equipped to grapple with the likes of the 49ers and Seahawks down the stretch.

The Silver and Black's crash landing after a 3-0 start revealed a fundamental truth about the franchise: This roster is still a long way off from competing in the AFC West. Credit first-year coach Klint Kubiak with finding ways to try to mitigate the myriad shortcomings. But the midseason pivot to No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza marked a fitting inflection point for a franchise that's now focused on reaping long-term rewards. The rookie quarterback, however, faces an inauspicious setup with a stalled-out run game and defense that has given up 30 or more points in five consecutive games.

This is going to be the grouping for the entirety of the NFC South, which seems stuck in football purgatory. Todd Bowles' defense, which now leads the NFL in EPA per play allowed, did a nice job righting the ship. But it remains to be seen whether offensive coordinator Zac Robinson can actually deploy Baker Mayfield as a value-added resource rather than something to be worked around, particularly after the quarterback's return from a dislocated right thumb. If anyone looks poised to take command of the league's most moribund division, however, it might be Tampa Bay.

Bryce Young finally brought out the explosive side of Carolina's offense. Then, everything else detonated for the Panthers, who are mired in a three-game skid. An iffy pass-protection setup has fully broken apart, with Young taking 14 sacks during the losing streak. The biggest disappointment, however, has been the unraveling of the defense. Perhaps the decimation of the injury-ravaged secondary was merely too much to overcome, but the decision to fire highly regarded coordinator Ejiro Evero on Oct. 30 demonstrated that the team clearly expected more out of this unit.

Atlanta briefly came back to life for what first seemed like an ill-fated three-week residency in prime time. But the Falcons have dropped four of their last five games, with a surprising takedown of the battered 49ers being the only outlier result during that stretch. It's fitting that a team led by Michael Penix Jr., the league's ultimate mystery-box quarterback, would prove so difficult to pin down. Trading away safety Jessie Bates III seems to indicate that general manager Ian Cunningham and president of football Matt Ryan believe the best iterations of this group are in the years to come.

A fairly uninspiring start to the season has served as a reminder that the worst-to-first projections were largely a reflection of the division rather than the Saints. Ultimately, Kellen Moore's crew doesn't have much to hang its hat on in Year 2 of the coach's tenure. Maybe the offense can reach a new level with running back Travis Etienne, who's played in just three games due to a hamstring injury, finally nearing a return.

In their surprising three wins to date, the Cardinals have proven themselves capable of punching above their weight class. That's an encouraging development in Mike LaFleur's first year, but there's still not enough of a clear core to have much confidence in what's been built to date. The final two months of the season might be a bit dodgier with Carson Beck taking over the offense, but at least a team with no clear path forward at quarterback will get a robust assessment of its third-round rookie.

What exactly can Dallas be confident about at midseason? It's certainly not the defense, which has made minor strides in recent weeks but still shows major vulnerabilities (including ranking last in third-down stop rate)? Meanwhile, the offense that was supposed to be the engine behind this group is stalling out with alarming frequency. Brian Schottenheimer's group has now authored two of the season's most embarrassing collapses and often shows a disregard for details. The Cowboys are somehow still a factor in the chase for the NFC East crown, but the wide-open nature of the division further underscores the missed opportunity here.

With a new regime driving home that wins and losses can't capture the progress of a teardown project, Miami makes for a difficult team to measure. At first glance, there aren't many areas that seem settled on a roster rife with holes. But first-year coach Jeff Hafley has clearly instituted a sense of determination in a group that, for all its deficiencies, hasn't lost by more than 10 points in a game since Week 3.

C.J. Stroud has slung Houston out of its early slump by propelling the team to wins in three of its last four games. Yet DeMeco Ryans' crew might still have too steep of a climb to re-enter the AFC playoff picture without some massive help. The dissolution of the back end of the defense is tough to swallow, while the offensive front's lack of push for a do-nothing ground game has left general manager Nick Caserio at a loss for answers. While surrendering the AFC South crown to Jacksonville last year felt like a possible one-season aberration, it now seems plain to see that Houston is no longer the class of the division.

More: Vikings' Kirk Cousins deal might doom NFC West: NFL trade deadline winners, losers

It's never a good sign when postgame news conferences become a matter of sussing out blame for late-game meltdowns. That's pretty much become the expectation for Washington, though. Dan Quinn and Co. have done little to wash away the foul taste of last season's disappointing follow-up to an NFC championship game run, leaving the distinct sense that this staff is on borrowed time, barring a sharp turnaround.

It's tempting to give Baltimore a pass on this season given how Lamar Jackson's injuries have derailed Jesse Minter's inaugural campaign. Yet the Ravens clearly were counting on a quick revival, and they've done little to support that cause. Minter hasn't brought the cohesiveness and cleanliness that were hallmarks of his Chargers defenses. In all, not nearly enough has changed in what was supposed to be a new era for the organization.

A calamitous run of injuries has unquestionably informed Philadelphia's ongoing seven-game losing streak. So, too, has the collapse of the infrastructure that once entrenched the Eagles as a lead NFC contender for the last half-decade. And personnel hits alone can't account for just how discouraging first-year offensive coordinator Sean Mannion's system has been, with the run game never truly taking root. Good on Howie Roseman for seeing what's brewing and equipping himself with plenty of resources – 10 picks in the first two rounds over the next three years – for a reboot.

In hiring Robert Saleh and bringing on a horde of high-priced free agents, Tennessee seemed to be aiming for a rapid revival. Once that notion fizzled, the Titans seemed to embrace a longer timeline for establishing competitive relevance by trading away Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker. At least Cam Ward has finally exhibited some heartening progress, though the team can hardly feel settled about where things stand for the 2025 No. 1 pick.

At least they eventually concluded this season was a lost cause, even if that realization came about 10 months too late. Dropping general manager Chris Ballard and shedding several key contributors on expiring contracts were necessary measures for a rebooting team with limited draft capital. Keeping running back Jonathan Taylor, however, was an odd move for a franchise that no longer looks positioned to capitalize on his prime.

Sitting at 2-7, Aaron Glenn maintained this week that the Jets feel as though they're "right on the cusp of trying to break through." Some evidence of that supposed trajectory would be nice. Frustrations have led Garrett Wilson and Geno Smith to near their boiling points in recent weeks. Meanwhile, the defense Glenn intended to supercharge with his play-calling is on the brink of collapse after a disastrous October. Perhaps worst of all: Gang Green has an ugly track record of coming through when it counts, whether it's in the red zone or at the end of either half.

Did you ever imagine you might see Jim Harbaugh robbed of his joy when discussing football? That's the toll that the Chargers' 0-8 start has taken on their typically ebullient leader. It's still hard to square how a team that won 22 games in the first two years of Harbaugh's tenure has managed to bottom out so quickly, though offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel's scheme has been nothing short of a disaster for Justin Herbert and Co. Perhaps worst of all, however, is Los Angeles' aversion to pursuing any meaningful in-season change, from the refusal to enact a staff shake-up to the incomprehensible decision to hold firm at the trade deadline. With a clear deleterious effect in play, this season might not be able to be simply flushed by the organization once it's over.

#2702. Should the Phoenix Suns make a trade for Domantas Sabonis or Paolo Banchero?

Ten games into the 2026-27 NBA season, the trade rumors are already swirling around the Phoenix Suns.

While a vocal segment of the fanbase cries out for a point guard like the oft-injured Darius Garland, a new round of players have been linked to the Suns, amid questions of fit in their starting lineup.

After a couple of rounds of forced trades, from Deandre Ayton to Kevin Durant, and the financial strain of the Bradley Beal dead money, the Suns find themselves with a redundant starting lineup comprised of the best that their circumstance dictated they could get. This led to a lineup simultaneously redundant and lacking. Issues with size, consistency, and fit continue to hamper the Jordan Ott and the Suns as they struggle to allow their highest-dollar players to shine without drowning out the production of their teammates.

Last season ended with Brooks and Green eating up shots in the playoff series against the Thunder as Devin Booker was reduced to spraying the ball out of double teams and when Jalen Green or Dillon Brooks got hot it the ball got stuck leaving Book looking to box out instead of repositioning for a new angle of approach.

This season Booker is finding his shot. Against the Spurs, Book went on a vintage scoring heater, but down the vine the other grapes withered and dried like raisins in the sun, with only the Suns rookie Malauch notching over ten points for the night. Miles Bridges noted in the press conference that Booker got hot. A similar explanation Booker gave in the Thunder series after Jalen and Dillon put up big shot numbers in a loss. An alarming lack of synergy even early in the season.

The national media has picked up on the narrative and turned it into trade talk as Bleacher Report connected the Suns to four potential trade candidates: Darius Garland, Anthony Davis, Domantas Sabonis, and Paolo Banchero.

While none of these players are without their flaws, an argument could be made for each of them to be added to the Suns. But I urge fans to remember that the Suns are owned by Mat Ishbia, whose ownership style could be summed up in one word. Aggressive.

So while you may see a million Twitter posts arguing for which of the four would best improve the Suns' chances at winning a first-round playoff series, I say no. That's not enough, like Warren G's third album, I Want It All. Or at least half of it. Let me present my most recent fix for the Phoenix Suns roster woes.

Anthony Davis is a day away from street clothes every day. While the upside is clearest and highest on this list, I remind you that the most recent Suns' finals appearance was largely related to the availability of their key players. They rode that injury luck to a 2-0 lead in the NBA Finals before it finally caught up with them and Dario Saric went down, taking with him the Suns' best hope at closing out the Bucks. If there was one trade that had a chance to make the Suns a true title contender, it could be Anthony Davis, but history would suggest it's more likely he watches the Suns flounder from the bench.

Darius Garland trade rumors and mock trades have made their way around Suns Twitter since last season and continue to color me unimpressed by the proposition. The Suns have aligned themselves to be a defensive team. They traded away two of their best shooters in order to pursue a top-tier defense, and even if Garland was driving and kicking to open shooters, who would he be kicking it out to? It would be Book, Brooks, and Bridges instead of Grayson or Royce. There would be nights that will work, but plenty won't, and consistent three-point shooting won't be something the Suns can rely on to show up in four or five games of a seven-game series.

This leaves us with Sabonis and Banchero.

In the off-season, I explored the possibility of a Domantas Sabonis trade and was roundly derided as a lunatic by those who were curious enough to click the article. Now they all come crawling back as the Suns' rebounding woes, lack of size, and youth at the center position make a Sabonis trade far more palatable to the Suns masses.

I view Sabonis as a starting center-sized version of Oso Ighodaro. He sets great screens, facilitates like Oso, but brings more firepower scoring the ball and has long been one of the best rebounders in the game. Despite his individual defensive concerns, with the number of communication breakdowns leading to the Suns' defense giving up way too open shots, it could be argued that a veteran presence like Sabonis could initially improve the defense and the KhOso tandem gains experience.

While they may have to wait until the trade deadline, the trade I originally proposed of Jalen Green and Mark Williams still sounds like a winner in early November. While Sabonis would bring much-needed experience, size, and positional flexibility, allowing him to play next to the Suns' young centers, it wouldn't fix maybe the most glaring need of the Phoenix Suns alone. The need for a second star next to Booker.

Fall where you want on the PG debate, but I continue to side with the faction that believes the problem isn't necessarily the lack of a point guard but a second advantage creator next to Booker when teams try to take him off the board. Paolo, while once one of the bright young stars in the league, has fallen out of fashion in the NBA fan community. Yet, outside of Davis, he represents to me the most realistic chance of landing a bona fide All-Star next to Devin Booker.

Banchero's size, versatility as a ball handler, and ability to score inside the paint would flourish in the shadow of Book's gravity. Much like the Suns have struggled to assemble and retain the right mix of players around Devin Booker, the Magic couldn't add the shooting it needed to free up Paolo's downhill game. A fresh start and new roster could resurrect his once-rising star.

Adding both of them together could be the Suns' best option to meet Ishbia's lofty goal of a second-round playoff appearance in the once-again hotly contested Western Conference, so I hopped on the trade machine to cook up a new look for the Suns. One that plugs some holes in rebounding and facilitation and adds some much-needed upside to the Suns' playoff prospects in the 2026-27 season.

In order to complete the trade, the Suns must wait until some of their recently acquired players become eligible to move, but when February 11th hits, this is what I think the Suns should do.

Projected Suns' starting lineup: Collin Gillespie / Devin Booker / Ryan Dunn / Paolo Banchero / Domantas Sabonis.

I see a roster with improved facilitation, rebounding, inside scoring, and three-point shooting, with Collin and Dunn getting their chance in the starting lineup. Banchero finds a new opportunity in the space created by Booker's presence and Collin's shooting, while Sabonis gets his first opportunity at legitimate playoff success, since the Kings took the Warriors to seven games in a first-round loss.54 wins and the 5th seed.

Let me know what you think in the comments.

#2700. How did Ohio State allow its quarterback room to reach this point?

There have been many issues plaguing Ohio State over these last two weeks.

The Buckeyes have seemingly come apart at the seams, struggling mightily in all three phases of the game. While the issues on defense and special teams are incredibly concerning in their own right, the injury to Julian Sayin has also unearthed some major flaws on the offensive side of the ball.

Of course, nobody would blame Ryan Day and Arthur Smith if the Ohio State offense experienced some setbacks after losing their starting quarterback. That said, I don't think many would have expected the drop-off to be quite as steep as it has been these last two weeks.

It is not the fault of backup quarterback Luke Fahey. The true freshman was not expected to be starting games for the Buckeyes in year one, or possibly even at any point in his career. It is clear that the California native is not ready to lead this Ohio State offense, but it is unfair to put the blame on his shoulders.

That blame falls on the Ohio State coaching staff, who have failed to plan ahead, failed to prepare, and failed to adjust to this new era of college football.

Ohio State is not the only program to lose its starting quarterback to injury, in general, but also this season specifically. They are, however, floundering in the wake of that injury more than others at this level.

The Buckeyes just got run out of their own building by an Oregon team that lost a potential first overall pick in quarterback Dante Moore. The Ducks' situation is a bit unique, and backup Dylan Railoa is far from perfect, but Dan Lanning and his staff had a competent quarterback ready to go in the wake of Moore's injury.

Look at what UCLA is doing this year. The Bruins are 9-0 despite losing starting quarterback Nico Iamaleava in their victory over Oregon in Week 5.

Backup quarterback Ty Dieffenbach, who spent last season at FCS Cal Poly, has helped lead UCLA to a perfect 4-0 record in his first four starts. Dieffenbach has thrown for 943 yards with six total touchdowns and two picks in those four games.

Even as recently as last season, Ole Miss lost starting quarterback Austin Simmons in Week 2. All backup Trinidad Chambliss did from there was total nearly 4,500 yards and 30 touchdowns while leading the Rebels to the College Football Playoff Semifinal.

These three programs were all able to field more than competent backup quarterbacks through vastly different methods.

Oregon paid up to get a flawed but talented player with hopes they could develop him into a starter for next season. UCLA, in year one under Bob Chesney, found a solid backup from the FCS ranks and has found a way to make it work. Ole Miss added an athletic freak from Division II, built the offense around him, and turned him into a superstar.

If other programs across the country, who have far fewer resources than Ohio State in two of the three aforementioned cases, can piece things together without their starting QBs, why can't the Buckeyes?

Many will try to blame the NIL era for Ohio State's weak position group behind Sayin. It is admittedly tougher to build depth at any position when guys can get comparable money at lesser programs to start.

That said, there is no reason the Buckeyes couldn't have gone out and found a talented QB at a lower level that would leap at the opportunity to be one snap away from starting at Ohio State.

They could have gone out and tried to find a veteran player from a lesser program with experience that could have stepped up in this exact scenario. Instead, they went out and got Justyn Martin, a guy who played six total games at UCLA and Maryland and has zero chance of ever taking a single snap in Columbus.

Ohio State could have also paid up to try and keep Lincoln Kienholz in Columbus, who has looked very solid at Louisville this season with 25 total touchdowns, and owns an ACC-best 9.8 yards gained per pass attempt. It likely would have cost them quite a bit to convince him to stay as the No. 2 guy, but he would be a massive upgrade over the current situation.

The options themselves aren't really the point of contention. The biggest issue is that Day and his staff had a complete lack of foresight in the added risk of injury in what has now become a potentially 16-game season.

Ohio State, during a normal season, is basically playing a full NFL schedule's worth of games. Every additional game increases the chance that you will lose a few guys to injury, and that obviously includes your starting quarterback.

The Buckeyes failed to adapt the roster to reflect this change. Even outside of not having a capable backup, Ohio State didn't do anything this offseason in an effort to provide extra protection for Sayin.

Ohio State's offensive line was not great last season, and they brought all of those guys back this year while not adding a single player up front via the transfer portal. Tyler Bowen, the man in charge of that position group, has done a miserable job of developing the unit — which is to be expected when you hire the Virginia Tech tight ends coach to lead your offensive line.

The Buckeyes under Day have also very rarely taken the opportunity to get their backup quarterbacks valuable reps in blowout games. Tavien St. Clair, the five-star QB on the roster who was supposed to be the heir apparent to Sayin, totaled two pass attempts in 2025, and now can't find his way onto the field even as Fahey has struggled through his two starts.

Day had gotten lucky to this point that he never needed the backup quarterback to be ready to go, but that luck has since run out, and they are now getting exposed at the most important position on the field.

Which brings us to the final flaw in this whole process: development.

Ohio State had an incredible run of quarterback play when Ryan Day was solely in charge of the position. From Dwayne Haskins to Justin Fields to C.J. Stroud, the Buckeyes were among the best in the country at the position through Day's first five seasons at the helm.

As Day shifted into more of a CEO role, Ohio State put a glorified intern, Corey Dennis, in charge, resulting in a down season at quarterback with Kyle McCord in 2023. The Buckeyes quickly rectified that issue by allowing Chip Kelly to take over when he got the offensive coordinator job, and Will Howard had a great campaign in 2024.

Beginning in 2025, the quarterbacks coach has been Billy Fessler, a guy whose only prior experience as a full-time QB coach is two seasons at Akron and one at UCLA. His one season with the Bruins in 2024 resulted in starter Ethan Garbers throwing a conference-worst 11 interceptions.

Clearly out of his depth, Fessler did nothing to help develop Sayin this past offseason. The Ohio State starter didn't make any sort of improvement from year one to year two, and was basically the same exact player we saw last season. Sayin was good, but suffered the same flaws in big games as he did in the 2025 postseason.

Now, with the Buckeyes desperately needing someone else to be ready to step up, nobody is.

Ohio State has a 6-foot-5 five-star on its roster at quarterback, and he is apparently so far from being ready to play that he remains on the bench behind a 5-foot-11 true freshman who was a former three-star prospect. The Buckeyes are going to continue to roll with Fahey over St. Clair, which is a clear failure of development from both Day and Fessler.

Ohio State should never find itself in this position.

Ryan Day came to Ohio State as a quarterback guru, and now one injury at the position has completely derailed an offense that still features the best player in program history at wide receiver, a running back who ran for more than 1,000 yards as a freshman last season, and several other highly touted skill players.

There are no excuses for the Buckeyes to look this unprepared. Ohio State has far too many resources at its disposal to let things get this bad this quickly at a premier position like quarterback, especially given that it is the position that gave the head coach his reputation in the first place.

Ovechkin has 38 goals and 33 helpers.

The 39-year-old Crosby is in the final year of his contract but has said he has no plans to retire. He and Ovechkin have joined Howe, Alex Delvecchio, Stan Mikita and Steve Yzerman as the only players in NHL history to play 22 seasons with one franchise.

"Over the years, obviously, I've developed a friendship with him and have a ton of respect for him," Crosby said to the media Monday with the Ovechkin news. "It's tough, you come into the league at 18 years old, and before we even met, we were built up against each other."

It should be Logan Thompson in net for Washington, and he was excellent in his season debut in allowing two goals in a win at defending Stanley Cup champion Carolina last Friday. Last season at home, he was 19-9-5 with a 2.18 GAA and three shutouts. Thompson made two starts vs. Pittsburgh overall last campaign and won both with a 1.50 GAA.

The Penguins and Capitals have three meetings left, including Washington's home finale on April 4. That should be quite the Sunday night if both Crosby and Ovechkin are healthy then. Tickets on the secondary market are north of $800 to get in.

We look for any edges in the slog that is the early NHL season, and you'd think the Caps want to send Ovechkin out a winner in his last home opener. And I prefer betting teams in their home openers anyway, simply riding the emotional wave. I hope both Ovi and Crosby score a goal, but that's not something I'd parlay. #2698. Neemias Queta is eager to give Celtics more without neglecting his core duties

Four games in six nights across four different cities, capped off by a back-to-back. For Celtics center Neemias Queta, that required 22.5 minutes per game, including a season-high 31 minutes in Wednesday night's road trip finale against the Raptors in Toronto.

Initially, Queta had no clue where to credit his critical source of energy.

"Not sure. I'm not sure," Queta told reporters after Boston's 98-93 win over Toronto, per CLNS Media.

But then, after shaking his head and cracking a smile as he thought about it, Queta credited those around him for their contagious approach.

"I think it's also energy plays from other teammates," Queta said.

Queta continued: "A lot of guys were making energy plays that galvanize your teammates, and we kind of fed from each other. And that's something we need to do more. It'll get us over the hump most nights."

The Celtics were without Paul George, their second-leading scorer, in Toronto as the 36-year-old sat out due to an illness less than 24 hours after dropping 36 points on the Sixers in Philadelphia. So that meant Boston had to pivot. Early on, however, it looked as though their first trip to The Six was shaping up to be a scheduled loss, despite the Raptors also being shorthanded without Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes.

TORONTO, CANADA – NOVEMBER 11: Jakob Poeltl #19 of the Toronto Raptors take a tipoff against Neemias Queta #88 of the Boston Celtics in the first half of their NBA game at Scotiabank Arena on November 11, 2026 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Cole Burston/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Boston's inability to contain Toronto's transition attack throughout the first half dug the Celtics into a hole, as they trailed by 22 points with 5:24 remaining until halftime. The Celtics responded with a 17-2 run of their own, cutting Toronto's lead down to 61-54 and giving the PG-13-less C's another chance to claw their way back with plenty of time to spare.

Still, there was plenty of more work to do.

Queta took only four shots throughout the night, including his third 3-point make of the season in the first quarter. He scored 11 points but recorded his first double-double of the campaign with 13 rebounds, which proved invaluable for the Celtics down the stretch.

He attempted four 3-pointers during the preseason, and has matched that total across the first 12 games of the regular season. It's something Queta truly believes he can work on, improve at, and add to his arsenal. But he's also aware that as a center, he still has fundamental responsibilities. So while pursuing that 3-point shot — among other strides — Queta understands he can't forsake his obligations to Boston's frontcourt.

"I think the game is so unpredictable nowadays that, like I've been saying over and over again, the more complete I can be, the more versatile I can be, the more I can play off others and they can be their best versions," he said. "I understand my teammates, and I can give them a relief in different aspects of the floor. Now it's just about me becoming more consistent in those things, whether it's shooting the ball, whether it's making reads with the ball in my hands, whether it's driving to the rim. I still need to be better."

In the final minute, Queta's commitment to those responsibilities became particularly valuable.

With less than 10 seconds on the shot clock, Jayson Tatum drove, drew two Raptors defenders and spotted Queta cutting to the basket for a wide-open dunk. That brought the Celtics within striking distance, trailing Toronto 93-92 with 54.1 seconds remaining.

TORONTO, CANADA – NOVEMBER 11: Jayson Tatum #0 of the Boston Celtics helps up Neemias Queta #88 in the second half of their NBA game at Scotiabank Arena on November 11, 2026 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Cole Burston/Getty Images) | Getty Images

After Tatum knocked down back-to-back free throws on Boston's next possession, Queta's next — and biggest — heroic moment arrived, one that ultimately made all the difference for the Celtics.

He secured a crucial rebound after RJ Barrett missed his go-ahead layup attempt, preserving Boston's 94-93 lead. The Raptors immediately fouled Queta, sending him to the line, where he knocked down both free throws to extend the Celtics' lead to 96-93 with 15.1 seconds left.

That rebound wound up being a game-saver for Boston, helping the team extend its winning streak to five games and tie the Lakers for the NBA's best record at 10-2.

"He continues to get better and better as a player on both ends of the floor," Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla told reporters. "Honestly, his offensive presence is just as impactful. Those two big free throws that he hit down the stretch, catching the ball in the seam, making plays. Defensively, he just lifts us to another level with the rim protection."

Teammates remain encouraged by Queta's continued improvements, following up his biggest breakthrough last season as a first-time starter.

"Neemi's been great for us," Derrick White told reporters. "He's grown so much these last few years, and he's a beast on both ends of the floor. Honestly, we ask a lot out of him offensively, and he just seems to always be in the right place, right time. Just expanding his game so much. We have so much trust in him."

Queta currently leads the Celtics in rebounds (6.2) and blocks (1.2) per game. He's also already surpassed his previous career highs in 3-pointers made and attempted in a single season, going 3-for-4 thus far, with plenty of basketball still ahead.

"We're gonna keep on getting better," Queta said, "and that's the mindset I have."

#2697. NFL Week 10 Survivor/Eliminator Picks

The trade deadline is a weird time in the NFL. Some teams are making big changes, but football isn't like baseball — there is work to be done to incorporate guys into lineups and rotations. In baseball, sure, there might be some chemistry to form between pitcher and catcher or between shortstop and second baseman, but it's an individual game in a team sport. In football, you have to figure out how things work. That means that guys on new teams might not be excellent right away. And that makes this a particularly tough week making picks in NFL Survivor. Check out my Week 10 pick for Survivor contests. And while we're here, you can use our NFL Betting Model and our Bet Tracker to make a pick for yourself.

And remember — this game is "once you use a team, they're off the board," so it's not always just a matter of taking the team you think will win. There has to be some strategy. I can't pick a team I've picked before, but you might not have tailed me, so previously used teams are eligible until the end.

#2696. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2695. Broncos, Giants, Browns among teams proving that winning ugly might be good enough this season

Everyone wants to be the mid-1980s 49ers or 1999 Rams, blowing teams out and making their seasons into beautiful highlight reels.

In the NFL in 2026, that might not be possible. Just grinding out wins is good enough.

There are four teams this season who have a winning record despite a point differential of +12 or worse: Broncos, Giants, Patriots, Browns. The Browns are 5-4 despite a point differential of -35. The Broncos have won seven games and six of them came by one score. They barely beat the 0-7 Chargers in Week 5 after trailing with less than 10 minutes remaining.

But they're winning. All of those teams would be in the playoffs if they started today other than the Browns, who are one spot out of an AFC wild-card spot. Other teams like the Steelers and Packers haven't been impressive from Week 1 on, but they're in the playoff field too.

"We found a way to win," has been uttered more than a few times by head coaches of winning teams this season. Winning ugly might end up being the theme of this season.

Head coach John Harbaugh of the New York Giants and Tyrone Tracy Jr. embrace after an overtime win over the Texans in Week 5.

The Giants' 19-11 win over the Eagles in Week 9 sums up how a handful of teams are succeeding this season. The Giants got four field goals and their only touchdown came when Jameis Winston came in off the bench for a drive. From an outside perspective, it was an unwatchable game. But it was pretty good for the Giants.

"We did play winning football, not perfect football, but winning football and found a way to win the game in all three phases, especially starting with the defense," Giants coach John Harbaugh said, via Athlon Sports.

The Giants beat the Titans, who are 1-7, when they intercepted a pass in their own end zone in the final seconds. They beat the Cardinals, who are 3-6, when they intercepted a pass backed up in their own end zone on the final play. The Giants rank 24th in DVOA but are currently the No. 3 seed in the NFC with a 5-2-1 record. For old-school football fans who abhor analytics and care only about a team's record, there's satisfaction in teams winning in intangible ways.

"They have it. They have what it takes," Harbaugh said of his team. "I don't know how to describe it other than that. I think they've had it all along and they found it in these games. Sometimes it's one thing to have it and another thing to find it, and they've been able to find it in the way they play."

The Browns are one spot below the Giants in DVOA, ranking 25th. But they've won more than they've lost. In multiple games this season they've discovered the right answer to the test in the final minutes. In four of five wins they've trailed or been tied in the final two minutes, and in the other win they trailed with four minutes remaining. They're 3-2 in games in which they gain 272 yards or less.

"We don't do anything, and then all of a sudden we get stops," Monken said after a 13-10 win over Baltimore, via the Ravens' site. "All of a sudden we figure it out."

These teams are chasing playoff berths, not trying to hear arguments about regression.

Since the start of the 2025 season, the Broncos are on one of the strangest runs in recent NFL history.

The Broncos are 22-6, counting postseason, and 18 of the wins have come by one score. For those who understand probability, and one-score games in the NFL being practically a coin flip, that record makes no sense.

The Broncos are 7-2 with a point differential of +12. That might be unsustainable, but they did it last season, too. The Broncos have won 16 one-score games in a row, setting an NFL record. That can't continue, but the Broncos truly believe it can.

"Well, when it keeps happening, I think our league is what it is," Broncos coach Sean Payton said after a 26-21 win over the Panthers. "When those things keep falling your way, that's not by accident."

Other teams looked terrible in September and have emerged as contenders for division titles. Packers fans had Matt LaFleur on the hot seat after a bad Thursday night loss to the Falcons dropped them to 1-2. The Steelers were 2-2 after four games and didn't look anything like a playoff contender, but haven't lost since. The Patriots were in trouble at 1-2 and while a blowout loss to the Packers last week was a setback, they're above .500 despite a win differential of just +4.

There might not be a more oft-used quote in the NFL than Bill Parcells' famous line, "You are what your record says you are." And, in truth, the win-loss record is all NFL coaches and players are judged upon. So nobody with a winning record now is making apologies, even if all those victories haven't been pretty.

#2692. Week 10 NFL picks against the spread, predictions for every game: Kirk Cousins returns to lead Vikings vs. Packers

It wasn't that long ago that Kirk Cousins, in his first stint with the Minnesota Vikings, was the quarterback who could never win the big one. Everyone remembers this critique of him.

These days, Kirk Cousins is 38. And somehow, everyone spent days and weeks arguing that the only way for the Vikings to have a chance to win the big one was to trade for Cousins.

That trade did happen, and it was perfectly reasonable for the Vikings to see if Cousins can guide them to an NFC North title and maybe a playoff run. They have the defense for it but we saw on Monday night that the offense was beyond repair with the quarterback situation they had. Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell was hesitant to announce Cousins would start Sunday against the Green Bay Packers, but the Vikings didn't trade for Cousins to watch Kyler Murray or Carson Wentz start in a huge divisional game.

While the trade for Cousins was reasonable, the Vikings still have the fourth-best quarterback in the division and the fourth-best offense in the division as well. Cousins is an upgrade but mostly because the Vikings had a dreadful quarterback situation.

The Packers didn't do anything at the trade deadline but it might be because they've been on quite a roll. They were not good through three weeks but somehow have emerged as one of the better teams in the NFL since then. Since Week 4, they're fourth in EPA (expected points added) per play on offense and third in EPA per play allowed on defense. It's a good team.

Anyone will have issues with the Vikings' defense and we'll see if the Packers' deep passing game can function against Minnesota's many blitzes. But Packers -3 is the pick. Taking the Vikings and Cousins, five days after rejoining the team, against a red-hot team is too much to ask.

New Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) shown facing the Packers in a 2023 game.

Here are the rest of the picks against the spread for Week 10 of the NFL season:

The Giants are three games up on the Commanders in the NFC East, but New York isn't that great. The Commanders come in as the more desperate team. Their season is all but over if they lose on Thursday. That's not the best reason to pick a team, but it's good enough in a game between two flawed teams.

This is the NFL's last early-morning game of the season. The Lions and Patriots meet in Germany. The Patriots are coming off a bad loss to the Packers, and have their running back issues with Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson out. One factor to consider is the Lions aren't the same team outdoors. Jared Goff's rating in domes is 102.9 and outdoors it is 92.4. There is some noise in those numbers, and Goff's ratings haven't had that big of a gap the past two seasons, but Detroit also just scored 19 points at Miami last week. That and the Lions' defensive deficiencies are enough to take the Patriots and the points.

The Browns have a better record, but also a -35 point differential. It's not like the Texans have been great, but there's a path for them to make the playoffs. They also know they can't drop games like this one. C.J. Stroud is playing well enough that points shouldn't be too hard for Houston to come by.

The Jaguars have taken over as my Super Bowl pick after the deadline. However, 10.5 is a lot of points in the NFL and the Titans have played three close games in a row. They're coming off their bye and have some extra rest. The Jaguars can't blow everyone out, right?

It's very hard to take the Colts, especially because the Dolphins are playing hard. The Colts played hard last week, but have to be deflated after losing that game to the Cowboys in the final minutes and seeing more players traded away. But it's even harder to back new Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord, a 2025 sixth-round pick who has never taken an NFL snap, playing with a subpar group. McCord gets the start for Miami with Malik Willis on injured reserve.

Talk about an ugly NFL side to take. The Jets are not good. But the Bills are coming off a physical game in Minnesota on Monday night and now go on the road to face the Jets on short rest. It seems unwise to take the Jets, but point spreads exist for a reason.

The Saints are probably better in theory than reality. They won last week, but needed to defend a two-point conversion in overtime to knock off Shedeur Sanders and the Browns. It feels like the Saints have the potential to be the best team in the NFC South, but there's not much evidence they are. The Panthers are in a slump but have been the better team.

It's not like the Falcons trading Jessie Bates III makes them significantly worse, but it's a difficult message for the locker room. It makes it seem like the front office is waving the white flag. In reality they got an offer they couldn't turn down, but it's still worth wondering how the remaining players will react. And Kansas City is a pretty good team.

For the rest of the season, or at least until Puka Nacua or Davante Adams returns, the Rams will try to survive by running the ball and playing defense in low-scoring games. There's not much explosiveness in the offense without any dangerous receivers. That will make them tough to back when the spread is large. Can Carson Beck lead the Arizona offense to enough points against a good Rams defense to cover any spread? That's the key question.

This isn't a pick due to Fernando Mendoza facing the Seahawks defense, though that is a factor. It's because the Raiders defense is horrible. #2691. Cavaliers 115, Knicks 107: “Credit them, but…”

As sports fans, our teams give us plenty to think about and then some. They give us stuff to bicker, to complain, to ramble about. We follow their every move meticulously, we break down the potential of prospective grocery baggers and hail them as the next coming. We love to read or listen to others doing the same, even or especially if we do not agree with their viewpoints. Lucky fanatics get something to cheer about every once in a while – consider that box checked by our beloved New York Knickerbockers lately.

Understandably, that focus on one team, that love for one franchise can lead to kind of a narrow view on things at times. Nothing wrong with that; fandom doesn't have to be rational, it doesn't have to explain itself. And it does not necessarily have to involve the other team's perspective or, frankly, the other team at all. At times though, that group in the different colored jerseys is the biggest answer to the question you have regarding your own squad's performance.

Last night felt exactly like that kind of game where the Knicks did a lot of stuff well, but in the end the Cleveland Cavaliers just did most of it a little bit better. And when the Knicks didn't do something as well, it was also the Cavaliers who had a hand in that. From the opening tip, it was obvious that the Cavs wanted this one – analytically and this time around actually in reality, too. They remembered last Saturday when New York rained on their Rocket Arena parade on the second night of a back-to-back; they surely remembered the last time they visited Madison Square Garden. And it looked like they were tired of the narrative that had them as the soft wannabes that can't keep up when the orange and blue drivers push the pedals to the metal.

Donovan Mitchell lived in the lane for most of the night; every high slip screen was an automatic downhill and kick opportunity for the team from Ohio, and their old and new length bothered the smaller Knicks for long stretches of the game. Peyton Watson might not be able to hit the water from the Verrazzano Bridge right now, but he sure can impact a game defensively. A lot of the Ohioans were feeling good about themselves; Tyrese Proctor and Meleek Thomas gave youthful, quality energy off the bench. And then, of course, there was James Harden. That guy who is a poster child for a lot of ugly wrongs in the modern game, the one who has been awful all year long so far but decided to show up for this one and give his team a vintage performance in the very building he crapped the postseason bed in just half a year ago.

So even if, at least in Harden's case, it's hard to stomach, let's follow Knicks Fan in Jerusalem's proposal from the Postgame Thread that gave this text its headline. Let's credit the Cavaliers for a game well played, for shots hit, for storms weathered. But as the headline and our friend in Israel suggested, there's another side to the story, a "but". Tipping our collective cap to the Cavs sure doesn't mean the Knicks can't do a lot of things better in the future. Jalen Brunson had a good scoring game yet failed to deliver any rhythm to the offense. Too many times the ball just stuck on the perimeter (a particular problem for OG Anunoby right now), and there wasn't nearly enough off-ball movement to stretch a much bigger defense that wants you to finish over their size.

That size played quite a role in yesterday's contest, be it on the boards or in the passing lanes. Unfortunately, the Knicks won't get any taller, that's for sure. Mike Brown tried to counter Cleveland's length by going to Mohamed Diawara early in the absence of Jordan Clarkson. Mo had a nice drive and, in theory, could be a solution for physical matchup problems like this one, but clearly isn't there yet. The young Frenchman seems unsure about himself, plays hesitantly, and is missing the wide-open shots he knocked down in his sleep last season. His defense mostly looks good but not good enough to warrant a bigger role yet.

Aside from plenty of mental lapses, missing open shots was a problem for Josh Hart last night as well, but we excuse the veteran as he clearly had to shake off some rust after his injury break. That doesn't change the fact that his lack of consistent outside shooting can become an issue at times, especially against good teams that willingly put roaming defenders on him. Normally, he adds so many other intangibles that you can live with it in the bigger picture more often than not. In Mikal Bridges' case, though, well, what's there right now? Hounding defense? Don't see it consistently. A presence off the ball? Nope. Secondary scoring? Corner threes? Emotion? Desperation? Anything?

Bridges once again played an uneventful, meager 17 minutes in this one. Plenty of the other guards – Deuce McBride, Landry Shamet, and Tyler Kolek – currently do everything Bridges is paid for and actually a bit more. The longer this situation drags on, the louder Mike Brown will hear the question: When will you make a change to the starting lineup? It's easy to understand why he's reluctant; he sure doesn't want to create an internal problem by benching someone who did his part in winning a championship last year. But what if the problem is creating itself? There's a tipping point to everything.

For the Knicks, this game won't be one, and it shouldn't be. There might be some stuff to think about, though, going forward. Just like we want to have it as fans.

#2690. "We don't want that in our home" – Dortmund chief speaks out on Nmecha's controversial celebration and "Ballers in God" links

Felix Nmecha made plenty of headlines last weekend when he celebrated his brace against SV Elversberg by removing an imaginary crown from his head and placing it on the pitch.

The celebration has been linked to the 'Ballers in God' network, which LGBTQ+ organisations have classified as "Christian fundamentalist", and its 'The King's Return' campaign, leading to strong criticism from Borussia Dortmund's Supporters Council.

Nmecha himself has since taken to Instagram to address what he considers to be "misunderstandings" surrounding his goal celebration.

"My celebration is not intended to promote myself or any organization. Rather, it is about laying my "crown" before the soon coming King and pointing to Jesus, my hope and strength! My message has never been about promoting intolerance, discrimination, or hate in any form," he stated.

Borussia Dortmund president and German Football Association vice-president Hans-Joachim Watzke has now had his say on the controversy.

"It is the fan department's right to initiate such a discussion. I attended their annual general meeting on Monday. It was clear that a significant majority of those who took issue with parts of his celebration were in favour of raising the matter. That means we have to take it seriously and discuss it," Watzke said on the "colourFIELD tell-a-vision" podcast, via Bild.

The BVB president was keen to express his support for Nmecha as a person, while stressing that he has no issue with the midfielder expressing his Christian faith.

"I like Felix Nmecha very much. We have a very, very good relationship and speak to each other frequently. As a practising Catholic, I am also the last person who would want to forbid someone from praying. That is not what this is about at all. That is perfectly legitimate," Watzke stressed.

According to Watzke, the issue lies with the crown gesture itself, with Borussia Dortmund concerned about being associated with the 'Ballers in God' network.

According to research by, among others, ARD's "Monitor" programme, parts of the religious group hold homophobic and anti-LGBTQ+ views and describe abortion as "Satan's plan".

"The only question we are discussing with him concerns the second part of his celebration," Watzke explained.

"If he scores a goal and points his index fingers towards the sky, everyone knows that he wants to thank God. He can also make the sign of the cross if he likes. But placing the crown on the pitch is, of course, somewhat associated with 'Ballers in God'. I don't want to pass judgement on it. But looking at what they stand for, Borussia Dortmund's code of core values and the fundamental outlook of 'Ballers in God' are not entirely compatible.

"That is why people at our club, particularly in the fan department, have the impression that an attempt is being made to establish a link with 'Ballers in God'. We don't want that in our home."

Watzke also confirmed that he has spoken directly to Nmecha, encouraging the midfielder to consider dropping the celebration to avoid creating divisions among the fanbase.

"I told him: 'Felix, if you feel that it is dividing the fans, perhaps you might also come to the realisation that you should stop doing it because it is causing division.' He wants to think about it. We had a wonderful conversation with him. We spent an hour on a video call. That is where things stand now, and he will give it some thought. I hope we can find a sensible solution," Watzke said.

#2688. Why was the Daiyan Henley trade to Broncos rescinded?

The Los Angeles Chargers have had a season to forget. There was so much hype around Justin Herbert and the magic that he could do with offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel. Well, the hype is dead, and the Chargers are 0-8.

Many thought the Chargers might have a fire sale at the trade deadline and that some key players would be on the trade block. Rumors even suggested they could deal Herbert. They decided players like Khalil Mack and Ladd McConkey were off the table.

Los Angeles kept many of its players but agreed to trade Daiyan Henley to the Denver Broncos. Why did that deal get rescinded?

MORE: Predicting upsets in Week 10 of NFL season

Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley celebrates after defeating the New England Patriots. | Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images

The Los Angeles Chargers originally traded linebacker Daiyan Henley to the Denver Broncos for a fourth- and fifth-round pick. The trade didn't finalize because of a failed physical.

It was the only trade the Chargers actually agreed to, which surprised people given their record and the talent on that roster. Their front office must believe this is just a down year and they'll rebound next year. LA still has some big questions to answer, like whether they'll eventually land McDaniel or Jim Harbaugh.

Finding a decent quarterback in the NFL is hard, and they have a capable QB in Justin Herbert. The Chargers will have to decide whether to invest in the Oregon product as their QB of the future.

Henley had a hilarious reaction when the trade fell through.

The Chargers LB has 21 tackles and 0.5 sacks this season. Los Angeles will try to get their first win of the season against the Baltimore Ravens on Monday Night Football in Week 10.

#2686. Cowboys have weapons to challenge the 49ers

The Cowboys moved to 4-5 with a dramatic 27-23 win over Indianapolis and now return home for one of their toughest tests of the season. San Francisco is 7-1, but Dallas enters Sunday having won two of its last three and is coming off a very productive offensive yardage performance.

Sure, the Dallas offense had issues scoring which was hampered by penalties and two critical turnovers, but they still produced 508 total yards.

Dallas outgained the Colts 508-271 yards on offense, producing 329 passing yards and another 179 on the ground. The Cowboys averaged 7.2 yards every time they snapped the football.

CeeDee Lamb was almost unstoppable in Indianapolis. He caught 10 passes for 195 yards and a touchdown, his second-highest receiving total in an NFL game. He now has 904 yards and seven touchdowns this season. San Francisco also left its latest game with cornerbacks Renardo Green and Deommodore Lenoir both day-to-day with injuries. If either is limited, Prescott should waste no time looking toward Lamb.

Javonte Williams also reached the century mark against Indianapolis, carrying 20 times for 101 yards and the game-winning touchdown. He now has 629 rushing yards and nine rushing touchdowns this season.

Keeping that balance is crucial against the 49ers. It slows down the pass rush and prevents San Francisco from simply attacking Prescott every down.

On the 49ers defense, Nick Bosa returned against Las Vegas, while DeForest Buckner made his return to San Francisco. Yet the 49ers finished the game with zero sacks. San Francisco have only 15 sacks entering that game, which is fourth-fewest in the NFL. The 49ers have dangerous names up front, but Dallas has reason to believe Prescott can be protected.

As for San Francisco's offense, it's dealing with a major injury problem. Christian Kirk has been placed on injured reserve. Mike Evans is not expected to be ready for this week, while Deebo Samuel is only expected to return to practice Wednesday after missing time with a hamstring injury.

That doesn't mean San Francisco lacks weapons. Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle remain major problems. But taking established receivers away from Brock Purdy makes the job easier for a Dallas secondary that has struggled this season.

If Dallas wants to beat San Francisco, slowing McCaffrey has to be near the top of the list. The encouraging part is what happened last Sunday. Jonathan Taylor entered the game as Indianapolis' biggest offensive weapon. Dallas held him to just 46 rushing yards. That was one of the Cowboys' best run-defense performances of the season.

McCaffrey presents a different challenge because of his receiving ability, but Dallas has at least shown it can stop a high-level running back from controlling a game.

So sticking with the Cowboys defense, Quinnen Williams forced a fumble last week, and rookie safety Caleb Downs grabbed his first NFL interception to seal the victory in the final minute. That comes after the defense produced five sacks and two takeaways against Arizona.

The 49ers are the heavy favorite, but the Cowboys have weapons that give the team at least a puncher's chance.

Taylor Swift knows a thing or two about putting on a big show, and Travis Kelce apparently plans to use that to his advantage. The Kansas City Chiefs star joked this week that he might enlist his wife to help with future New Heights live events.

The topic came up as Jason Kelce recapped the podcast's latest tailgate in Philadelphia, which he called the best one the brothers have hosted. When Jason asked if Travis knew anyone who knew anything about stages, Travis had an obvious answer.

Swift has a history with the podcast, too. She made her first and only New Heights appearance in August 2025, announcing her album The Life of a Showgirl in what became the show's most-watched episode. The couple got engaged two weeks later and married in July.

On Wednesday's episode, Jason said that he wanted to bring the same setup to future events, but noted some logistical issues.

"If we can recreate this in other areas, I do think the stage is really important. The problem is most tailgates don't have a stage, so I don't know how we're going to do it," Jason said, on New Heights. "Anyways, maybe we build our own."

Then Jason turned to his brother. "Do you know anybody that knows things about stages?" he asked.

"Yeah, I actually do," Travis responded, before adding, "I'll see what my wife can cook up."

Jason then jokingly imagined how Swift would respond, saying, "I know the companies I deal with are not going to [mess] around with you dumb [expletives]."

Regardless, being married to one of the most famous artists on the planet might have its perks.
