#2651. John Harbaugh: tonight’s Commanders-Giants game “is for all the marbles” - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

The thing about firing Dan Quinn as coach of the Washington Commanders — though it would placate an increasingly dissatisfied fanbase — is there's a trickledown that would leave the franchise in a state that has defined it for far too long: unstable.

Bear with me, because a vote for the status quo could seem — how to put this? — wild at the moment. This isn't a case that Quinn should keep his job based on his team's current trajectory as much as it is a warning about what would follow if the losses continue.

When things are going as they are — and Washington is 4-15-1 over the last 13 months — people tend to want heads to roll. Change becomes the only way to satisfy that. It's an emotional response, which is fine, because what's the point in rooting for a sports franchise if it doesn't manage to tap into your emotions?

But think about the fallout if Quinn and his staff don't survive. Their fate hangs in the remaining results, which must start improving beginning Thursday night against the New York Giants at the Meadowlands. There are a host of reasons any Commanders fan who is interested in the long-term stability and success of the franchise should root for a turnaround.

[Josh Harris's] record in the other two American sports franchises he owns would suggest Harris isn't afraid of change. That's good. A willingness to admit mistakes should be a trait of a good owner.

But if Quinn is ousted after his third season, wouldn't the start to Harris' stewardship feel — and it's scary to go here — a little Snyder-esque?

The way to avoid that: Have Quinn and his crew turn this season around. At this point, that might seem unlikely, but in the interest of distancing this franchise from the previous quarter-century, it would be the best outcome for everyone — from the quarterback to the fans.

Daniels came into 2026 ready to reset after missing 10 games due to injury last season. The Commanders were also in reset mode. They kept head coach Dan Quinn in place, but swapped out both coordinators. On Daniels's side of the ball, they promoted David Blough to become their new OC and implement a more traditional, under-center style of offense—a significant change after primarily running a no-huddle, shotgun offense under Kliff Kingsbury. They also made numerous roster changes, primarily on the defensive side of the ball as they looked to improve one of the worst-ranked defenses in the NFL during the 2025 campaign.

The new offense has brought mixed results. There are times that Daniels and the offense are in rhythm, such as in the first half of their game against the Rams, when they got out to a 10–6 halftime lead. At other times, they struggle to move the ball at all, such as in the second half or their loss to the Rams, when they couldn't muster a single first down in the third quarter.

The Commanders' offense ranks 20th in yards per game (325.4) and passing yards per game (207.4), 21st in points per game (21) and 22nd in EPA per play (-0.08). They are undermanned due to injuries to their best offensive lineman, Laremy Tunsil, and receiver, Terry McLaurin, but also aren't fully playing up to their potential.

Aside from some game management miscues, Daniels is still playing well, even if he's not quite lifting the team the way he did as a rookie.

While McCarthy has changed teams and other quarterbacks from the class saw their teams undergo coaching changes early on (Michael Penix Jr., Caleb Williams and Drake Maye), Daniels could be facing that fate in Year 4 if the Commanders move on from Quinn.

The Commanders have their quarterback in Daniels, but with low playoff hopes (a win Thursday would draw them to two games behind the Giants in the NFC East, while the wild-card field is crowded) and a franchise still figuring out how to properly build around him, his career is at an odd standstill. He is not trending downward, but he has also not built off that wondrous rookie campaign.

The Nov. 1 game against the Philadelphia Eagles was the first after McLaurin suffered a season-ending torn patellar tendon. The injury was bittersweet for Burks. It gave the 26-year-old an opportunity to start, which he capitalized on with three catches for 81 yards in the win at Northwest Stadium. Seeing McLaurin go down, however, was gutting.

Burks's absence with a foot injury was felt in Washington's loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday, but Coach Dan Quinn said Burks will return when the Commanders (2-5-1) visit the New York Giants (5-2-1) on Thursday night. They need him to pick up where he left off — he has gone from a supplemental piece to a key cog.

While he has only played in six games, Burks is fourth on the team with 233 receiving yards. He leads Washington with 19.4 yards per catch and should see a higher volume of targets when healthy.

Everything has started to click for Burks. Coming off a stagnant performance against the Rams, the Commanders could use a big performance from him against the Giants. He no longer doubts his ability to do that.

"I'm playing backyard football again," Burks said. "My confidence was out of the roof — it still is out of the roof."

"They don't understand that the cornerback is a top-two hardest position to play in football," said the Washington Commanders starting … cornerback. "A lot of people can't — I don't even want to say a percentage, but not a lot of people can do it, right?"

That's an accurate assessment on the broad humans-interested-in-football scale. Even some capable ones cannot stick around for long. Robertson, a 2019 first-team All-American at Louisiana Tech and a 2020 fourth-round selection by the Las Vegas Raiders, is in Year 7. This is despite being the definition of undersized, even among the non-behemoths he shares the field with.

Generously listed at 5-foot-9, the 183-pound cornerback has the required coverage and ball skills; Robertson is tied for the league lead with nine pass deflections, according to TruMedia. But when it comes to why some thrive at the position regardless of their size and skill set, Robertson sees the importance of the mental game.

"You have to have a different kind of mindset because you can make a thousand plays, and you still can cause the team to lose," Robertson said. "Could be any critical moment. It could be a small first down that puts a team in field-goal range. Then they kick a field goal, and you lose the game. Everybody will say, 'Oh, it's your fault.'

The Giants are third in the NFL in passing defense, giving up only 177.8 yards per game, and fifth in total defense. They haven't been as strong, though, at stopping the run. New York is 21st in yards allowed per game, with 123.6 yards per game and 4.7 yards per carry. Washington is 11th in rushing offense and eighth in yards per carry despite injuries in the backfield. Jacory Croskey-Merritt was lost to an injured groin, while Jemery McNichols faces potential foot surgery two games after briefly returning from IR. Right now, the Commanders' running backs are Rachaad White, Austin Ekeler, and Robert Henry. And there's always the running threat of quarterback Jayden Daniels. Rachaad White showed flashes a week ago, but Washington needs to establish their ground game early and often to keep New York on its toes.

QB stat to know: Jayden Daniels has thrown seven touchdowns and no interceptions. This team has little margin for error, and turnovers would bury it. But this offense hasn't yielded the explosive results Washington discussed in the offseason. It's a new system for Daniels and, through the same amount of games his rookie season, he had six touchdowns and two picks — en route to 25 scoring passes.

Second-half storyline: Dan Quinn's job security. Washington's first-half schedule was difficult but it should be better than 2-5-1. Quinn also opted for first-time coordinators on both sides and that has led to growing pains. None of this has been ideal for a coach whose team is 7-17-1 since it went 12-5 in 2024. — John Keim

Here is one thing we know about the Giants' plans to beat the Commanders: they are going to put pressure on Daniels.

The Giants' defense has continued to improve from the last time the two teams squared off in Week 5. They are now fifth in yards allowed and third against the pass, allowing just 178 yards through the air. Part of that is a credit to how much pressure they put on opposing quarterbacks; they rank third in blitz percentage, according to Pro Football Reference, and considering that they pressured Daniels on nearly 30% of his dropbacks in Week 5, you can expect something similar in Week 10.

Here's the silver lining for the Commanders, though: while the Giants do blitz more than almost any team, it has not led to pressures. They rank last in pressure rate (18.9%) and only have 16 sacks for the season. In fact, rookie Arvell Reese is the only Giants defender with more than two sacks on the year.

Although it might not feel like it after allowing four sacks against the Los Angeles Rams, the Commanders are around league average in sacks allowed and rank sixth in pass block win rate, per ESPN. That isn't going to stop the Giants from trying, though, so it will be important for Washington's offensive line to give Daniels time to work. If the blitzes keep coming, there will be areas for him to exploit downfield.

I really want to believe in the Commanders. I picked them to upset the Los Angeles Rams last week, and it was an extremely even game. The Rams going 3-for-3 on fourth down and Myles Garrett being active decided the game. You could make a case that Dan Quinn's team got unlucky, but I won't do that. When something happens repeatedly, it's not luck. Unfortunately, losing close games seems woven into the fabric of the 2026 Commanders, perhaps as karmic payback for a 2024 iteration that seemingly won every close game and converted every fourth down en route to a surprise appearance in the NFC Championship Game.

The Giants are 4-1-1 in one-score games. That tie came against these Commanders in a game that Washington absolutely should have won — and I'm a Giants fan saying that. John Harbaugh is just a better coach than Quinn. It is what it is.

Obviously, the Commanders have the better quarterback. Daniels is still electric, and J.J. McCarthy was not good in the win at Philly. I just have faith that the Giants will make plays when they need to, and the Commanders not only won't but will actively hurt their own chances at winning.

What else is there to say about this offense? I keep sitting down to write these reviews hoping that the film will give me something different to discuss. Instead, the Eagles ended up with 220 yards of offense, 13 first downs, and an average of 3.3 yards per play. They had the ball for nine and a half fewer minutes than the Giants. Another week, another miserable offensive performance. Hooray!

Joe Milton gave us a few things to enjoy. His mobility prevented an already awful performance from looking even worse, and there were a couple of throws that showed why his arm talent is intriguing. But changing the quarterback hasn't changed how I feel watching this offense. It is still boring, disjointed, and far too difficult. At this point, I want this staff to move on so I can start looking forward to a new season. It's November! I'd like to feel excited about the Eagles' offense again.

Although it seemed at times that they would find a way to lose the game, the Dallas Cowboys managed to prevail over the Indianapolis Colts. It didn't exactly save a season that still is teetering on the edge of the precipice, and any good feelings from this win are likely to dissipate when Dallas host the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. Our Tom Ryle and Sean Martin take a look at what faces the Cowboys.

I have to compare the narrow 27-23 win over the Colts to cotton candy. We wanted it, but it turned out to be messy and rather unsatisfying.

And it didn't exactly presage a strong showing against the Niners, who are one of the best teams in the league. While Dallas has managed to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory more than once this season, San Francisco keeps finding ways to win with an injury list that runs on and on. They have a clearly winning culture, while the Cowboys have something. And there is absolutely no comparison between the head coaches.

If Dallas loses, especially by double digits, I think there will just be a sense of resignation and no expectations that the Cowboys can claw their way back into the playoffs.

The worst thing is how this all seems largely irrelevant. Not only have the Cowboys done nothing to really make us think they can win, they have also shown no carryover from a previous win.

And if they do lose, we can just relax and start digging into potential draft picks and replacements for the coaching staff.

Week 10 will be telling when it comes to the Giants' path to an NFC East title

[T]his week could provide a massive swing for the Giants.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh was speaking specifically about the Commanders when he said the following, but the idea he was getting at applies to the week and the division as a whole:

"This is for all the marbles. It's a tie right now. This is the tiebreaker. It's like going to the second half tied, you have a chance to go win the game right now and be one up on these guys for the rest of the season. So, it's a big game."

If the Giants lose Thursday and Dallas upsets the 49ers, this is what the NFC East would look like:

Dallas would be just 1.5 games back, and the Commanders would be back in the hunt with eight games remaining.

Rain. Low around 40. North wind 9 to 11 mph, with gusts as high as 23 mph. Chance of precipitation is 80%. New precipitation amounts between a quarter and half an inch possible.

The Giants lost a chance to win that game when a glove-less Skattebo fumbled away a scoring opportunity in overtime. The Giants have fumbled 14 times this season, losing six. Four teams have more fumbles than the Giants, with the Packers, Patriots, Chargers, and Saints all having 15.

Ball security will be at a premium Thursday night. That has, obviously, not been a Giants' strength this season. Thus, it is worth paying attention to.

Considering the likely conditions, it is also worth remembering that rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada went just 2 of 5 on field-goal tries against Washington the first time, missing from 50, 57, and 46 yards.

Teams have combined to score 45.93 points per game this season, according to NFL Research. That's down slightly from 46.74 points per game halfway through last season, and a tick higher than the 45.36 points per game after nine weeks in 2024.

The league has seen plenty of close finishes this season. Through nine weeks, 77 games have come down to one score (eight or fewer points). That ties the 2016 season for the third-most through Week 9 in NFL history, trailing only the 2024 (79) and 2022 (79) seasons.

Of those 77 games, 41 have featured a game-winning score in the final five minutes of regulation or overtime. That's the second-most through Week 9, trailing only the 2021 season, which featured 42 such finishes. In 25 games, the winning team rallied from at least 10 points down, which ties the 2011 season for the fourth-most in league history. That figure trails the 1987 (30), 2020 (26) and 2022 (26) seasons.

The NFL implemented its "dynamic kickoff" before the 2024 season to help the play regain relevance after years of teams booming the ball out of the end zone and settling for touchbacks rather than risking big returns.

The changes have seemingly done the trick, as the number of kickoff returns (1,118) and kickoff return yards (28,896) mark the most in league history through nine weeks.

We're in the throes of spooky season, and fittingly, the New Jersey Devils just got a lot scarier with the acquisition of superstar goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.

One of the best goaltenders in the world, Hellebuyck fills the biggest need on the Devils roster. With him in between the pipes and an electrifying group of forwards, New Jersey will be a force in the Eastern Conference.

Don't take my word for it. Just look at what the Devils did Tuesday against the Dallas Stars. In his first start with the team, Hellebuyck stopped 17 of the 18 shots he faced -- allowing one goal on 2.04 expected goals against -- in a 5-1 victory.

Nico Hischier, Jack Hughes and Luke Hughes each had multi-point nights as the Devils took full advantage of the chances they created against a stout Dallas team. This type of game has to be exactly what general manager Sunny Mehta envisioned when he swung the deal for Hellebuyck.

Moving forward, the Devils will be burdened with the pressure that comes along with being a bona fide Cup contender. For a franchise that's fallen short of expectations a few times lately, that can be a scary prospect, and it inspired a special Halloween edition of the NHL Power Rankings in which I highlight the scariest thing about each team.

#2649. How busy will the MLB offseason be before likely lockout? Insiders weigh in on November's urgency, uncertainty

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hot stove season is underway in Major League Baseball. And with a lockout looming when the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, the next four weeks will likely be the only time that teams have to sign free agents, make trades and reshape their rosters before transactions come to a halt.

Want some context into just how much of a mad dash this could become? One brief exchange with a head of baseball operations offered a glimpse. When asked what his club anticipated in the coming weeks, the executive offered only this: "I'm going to stiff arm you on this one," the exec said. "Because I'm time constrained right now. A lot going on with staff and player conversations."

Urgency will play a role this November. Naturally, teams don't want to be left behind. And the way modern baseball conducts business could be challenged.

Over the last five years, the early stages of MLB's offseason have been largely anticlimactic. Front offices, many of which rely on similar analytical models, have increasingly approached the market with caution, contributing to a process that can drag well into the winter.

Even the Winter Meetings, traditionally a gathering place in early December for blockbuster trades and significant free-agent signings, have increasingly become more of a launching pad for offseason conversations than a destination for completed deals.

So, what does this peculiar November have in store? Yes, there will be moves. But according to one high-ranking league executive, don't expect the approaches that have defined the modern offseason to change entirely. The urgency might be different, but the process of gathering information, evaluating talent and understanding the market remains largely the same.

"You can't get caught flat-footed, so we're going through the same motions of lining up who we like, identifying different ways to meet our needs, calling agents and letting them know we have interest," the executive said. "Next week at GM meetings will be helpful to learn more. That's usually when we indicate we want to zoom with a player and we'll see how agents/players react to that."

Trades, certainly, could take precedence over free-agent signings, given the circumstances and the talent available. This year's free-agent class is notably weak, particularly when it comes to starting pitching. The trade market, meanwhile, could offer alternatives that free agency simply doesn't.

One left-handed starter from the Los Angeles Angels, who isn't set to become a free agent until 2029, figures to be particularly coveted.

"A bunch of teams need pitching based on our initial sweepstakes," the executive continued. "So I think names like Reid Detmers will be in high demand. If you're a team in on him, it might be worth overpaying to jump the line. After [Tarik] Skubal, none of the starting pitching free agent names are that exciting."

No team wants to get left behind. But with the uncertainty surrounding 2027 and little indication of what next year might look like, teams don't want to overreact, either. The temptation to move quickly must be weighed against the consequences of making the wrong move.

Reacting to an opponent's moves, as that same executive suggested, can prove costly. Particularly in a market where the pressure to act could drive up the price of acquiring talent.

More importantly, all of this remains a moving target. The uncertainty surrounding the next season complicates even the most straightforward roster decisions. Rentals, as one front-office official put it, aren't particularly attractive given the circumstances. In the (still seemingly unlikely) event that there's no baseball in 2027, trading away prospects or valuable big-league talent for a player with only one year of control becomes a considerable gamble. A team could surrender valuable assets without ever getting the opportunity to benefit from the acquisition.

Years of contractual control carry even greater value now. Teams recognize that, which could ultimately stall trades. The very players who might offer the most security in an uncertain market could also become the most difficult to acquire.

"We're really operating under uncertainty now," one front-office person said.

Now, that isn't to suggest free-agent deals won't get done. In fact, one agent said he wouldn't be surprised to see a flurry of mid-tier players reach agreements ahead of the Dec. 1 CBA expiration, pointing to the activity leading up to the 2021–22 lockout as evidence of how an approaching deadline can accelerate an otherwise slow-moving market.

"Last time there was going to be a lockout it was extremely active for Kevin Gausman and Marcus Stroman, who were free agents entering 2022," the agent said.

Gausman signed a five-year, $110 million deal with the Toronto Blue Jays, while Stroman inked a three-year, $71 million contract with the Chicago Cubs. Corey Seager and Marcus Semien, meanwhile, agreed to huge deals with the Texas Rangers. A total of $1.7 billion in free-agent contracts were agreed to prior to the lockout.

This year, Sonny Gray, Tyler Mahle, and Gausman, again, certainly fit that second-tier group.

"Nothing motivates clubs more than a deadline, so I'd be shocked if there wasn't a flurry of deals prior to the deadline," the agent said.

Whether through trades or free agency, the expectation remains that deals will get done in the next four weeks. It will be a fascinating November.

#2648. Gattuso primo vincitore del Premio Corigliano: cerimonia a Coverciano per il tecnico della Lazio

Il riconoscimento istituito dall’Aiac sarà consegnato da Renzo Ulivieri il 16 novembre, durante la Panchina d’Oro 2026.

Rino Gattuso, attuale tecnico della Lazio, è il primo vincitore del Premio Ernesto Corigliano, istituito dall’Associazione Italiana Allenatori Calcio (Aiac). Secondo quanto riportato da LaC News24, La consegna è prevista il 16 novembre a Coverciano, in occasione della Panchina d’Oro 2026.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Sarà il presidente dell’Aiac, Renzo Ulivieri, a consegnare il riconoscimento a Gattuso. Il tecnico biancoceleste riceverà così la prima assegnazione del premio dedicato a Ernesto Corigliano.

Avvocato cosentino, Corigliano promosse la costituzione dell’Assoallenatori il 19 settembre 1966. Nel sessantesimo anniversario della fondazione, l’Aiac vuole ricordare «il contributo determinante» dato da Corigliano alla nascita di un’organizzazione unitaria degli allenatori, orientata alla tutela della loro professione.

#2646. Denny Hamlin Names 3 Races That Cost Him the 2026 Title, Blames Himself for 1

Denny Hamlin says three races cost him the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series title, and that one of the mistakes was his.

Hamlin looked back on the Chase on Actions Detrimental, his weekly racing podcast. He finished third in the final standings, 56 points behind champion Kyle Larson.

"We all know, right, that my Chase boiled down to two pivotal moments," Hamlin said. "Probably, I think in my mind, it was Las Vegas. Well, Darlington. Okay, okay, it's three. It's Darlington, it's Vegas, it's Phoenix, though."

"Those are the three tracks where we actually had winning speed. We were fast enough to win those, and those were where we got our worst results. And that is just a non-winning formula, right?" he said.

Darlington opened the Chase. A costly pit stop put Hamlin in traffic, and contact with Michael McDowell damaged his No. 11 Toyota. He finished 18th.

Hamlin does not think he caused that one. McDowell gave his side of the contact the following weekend, saying both drivers could have done better.

The October Chase race at Las Vegas was different. Hamlin said the team's pit call let Larson get back on the lead lap. Hamlin then spun while trying to regain ground.

"I didn't think I did anything wrong when I got hit by McDowell. I do think I did something wrong when I spun at Vegas," Hamlin said.

"But again, I was put in a tough spot, and then they were whipping the horse, saying, 'Go, go, go, get him.' And I'm like, 'All right, I'm gonna go.' And so, but that's still me," he said.

"They're not driving the car. I am," Hamlin said.

After Las Vegas, Hamlin defended his team over the pit call. Crew chief Chris Gayle explained the decision and took the blame for it.

At Phoenix, a tire failure ended a strong run. A pit-road speeding penalty also cost him a chance to get back on the lead lap, and he finished 28th. He still does not know what caused the tire to fail.

"And then the Phoenix tire, I mean, I don't know. Who knows? Is it us? Was it bad luck? I don't know," Hamlin said.

Hamlin entered the Chase as the top seed with a 25-point cushion after four regular-season wins for Joe Gibbs Racing. Under the new format, there were no elimination rounds, so every lost point carried forward.

He ran well in the finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway, winning Stage 2 and leading a race-high 87 laps. He finished sixth, while Larson clinched the title after Stage 1.

The 45-year-old has signaled that 2027 is likely his final full-time Cup season. He is still chasing his first Cup championship.

#2645. Bengals sent Zac Taylor to clear the Eagles’ name in failed Arnold Ebiketie trade

The Eagles and Bengals thought they had a deal in place to send Arnold Ebiketie from Philadelphia to Cincinnati, but just an hour after the trade was announced, it had reportedly been canceled. Insiders like Adam Schefter were quick to report that the trade falling apart was not due to a physical or performance concern, and it was eventually revealed to be a miscalculation on what Ebiketie would cost the team.

Initial trade terms was sending a sixth-round draft pick to the Eagles in exchange for the OLB, but since Ebiketie was a compensatory free agent, trading for him would negate the Bengals future third-round comp pick from the Trey Hendrickson trade. Adding in the loss of a third-rounder, in addition to the agreed upon sixth-round pick, made the trade to expensive for Cincinnati, so they bailed on the deal.

Instead of speaking to reporters about the incident himself, Bengals GM Duke Tobin sent a message via head coach Zac Taylor about the situation — who admitted he didn't really feel comfortable with the specific way Tobin wanted things portrayed —, but wanted it to be clear that Howie Roseman and the Eagles were good trade partners.

Mike Garafolo said that the vibes inside the Eagles building were very angry, and how teams move in these situations can absolutely affect future trades and team's willingness to do business together. Taylor shouldn't have been the messenger, but it was important for Tobin to clear the air and make sure this move wouldn't even further affect the Eagles in a negative way.

#2642. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2641. Brewers' Pat Murphy apologized to Yankees' Brian Cashman over viral comment about Jake Bauers free agency

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the aftermath of the World Series championship, Brewers manager Pat Murphy was caught on a hot mic talking to first baseman and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, who heads into free agency this winter off a career year.

Murphy's message? "You're gonna be a rich f---er, but just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself, just remember, say, 'this is the way we used to do it.'"

The comment, predictably, drew backlash from those who assumed Murphy was taking a shot at the Yankees. Bauers was on the 2023 Yankees, when they went 82-80 and missed the playoffs.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out," Murphy said on the New York Post's "The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman released on Tuesday. "I picked up a phone and called Brian right away, and had a good conversation. And the best I could try to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand. I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,' " Murphy explained. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us and you're going to forget all about how we did things. … I would just give him this rhetoric every time.

"I was just referring to the teams that have a lot of high-paid, long-contract players," Murphy said. "That sometimes it's harder to get all those guys together to play together. And I used the Yankees because I knew Jake was with them before. … I regret saying it, but that was Jake and I's humor behind the scenes and I got caught."

First off, dudes talking to dudes when they don't realize anyone else is listening lends itself to a lot of comments they don't necessarily mean or, perhaps more importantly, don't include the context of a longstanding relationship between a manager and his player. There isn't anything really out of line here in terms of the Yankees shot. Any Yankees fan would tell you they agree with Murphy's assessment of that team.

Where I do believe there's a problem is the insinuation that a player getting a huge payday means that he'll just start playing only for himself instead of doing things as a team. The Dodgers' high individual salaries certainly didn't stop them from winning two straight World Series titles.

Further, Bauers made $2.7 million last season, double his previous high. MLB players have a finite shelf life and need the money they make to stretch, if they're lucky, for generations. He's set to make exponentially more in free agency in his one big payday to hopefully set up his family for decades. Some might think it insensitive of Murphy to mock that a player might need to look out for himself and his family.

Then again, take note of Murphy's quote when he says that's just their sense of humor. We don't know their personal relationship because it is just that: personal. Unless Bauers signs elsewhere and comes out guns blazing against Murphy, this whole thing is probably just much ado about nothing. It would be pretty shocking if Cashman took particular offense, either.

#2637. Former Yankees, Rangers All-Star Mark Teixeira wins U.S. House seat in Texas

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Major League Baseball star Mark Teixeira is headed to Capitol Hill after winning the election for the United States House of Representatives seat in Texas' 21st district on Tuesday. Teixeira, the Republican candidate, beat Democrat Kristin Hook, a former federal scientist.

Teixeira will now take over the seat vacated by Republican Chip Roy, who didn't seek re-election.

"Together, we can build a better future for our families, our neighbors, and every community across Texas 21," Teixeira said in a statement. "I'm excited to get to work. I will be praying for all of you and for the future of this great nation. God bless Texas, and God bless America."

He was a rare win for the GOP in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the gubernatorial race and Democrat James Talarico flipped the Senate seat.

Teixeira, 46, was born and raised in Maryland before attending Georgia Tech as a big-time prospect. He was selected fifth overall in the first round of the 2001 Draft by the Rangers. He then came up through the Rangers' system and spent the first four and a half seasons of his career with the ballclub. He was traded to the Braves in 2007, then to the Angels in 2008 before signing a long-term free agent deal with the Yankees prior to the 2009 season. He finished his career with the Yankees.

In parts of 14 seasons, Teixeira hit .268/.360/.509 (126 OPS+) with 409 home runs, 1,298 RBI, five Gold Gloves, three All-Star Games, three Silver Sluggers and a World Series ring.

Teixeira is one of several familiar sports faces up for election on Tuesday. Former college football coach Tommy Tuberville won the Alabama gubernatorial race and former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya lost the Minnesota Senate race.

#2635. MLB rumors: The only Oriole not on the trading block, Rays' Drew Rasmussen plan and Astros add to manager hunt

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Brewers have now been World Series champions for just one week (minus a few hours) and they should still be basking in the glory for quite a while. As the offseason marches on, the next big date will be Nov. 17, when decisions on qualifying offers are due from the eight players who received one.

In the meantime, the rumor mill should be ever-so-slowly churning. We'll round it up here.

The Houston Astros moved on from general manager Dana Brown in August and fired manager Joe Espada after the 2026 season. Newly hired general manager Randy Flores is now tasked with landing a new dugout boss, and a three-time MVP and future Hall of Famer is in the mix. The Astros will interview Albert Pujols for the manager job this week, per The Athletic.

Pujols has long made it known that he desires to be an MLB manager. He recently interviewed for vacancies with the Padres and Angels (both last offseason) and he also managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic this past spring. It should be further noted that Pujols is in the fourth year of a 10-year, $100 personal services contract with the Angels that was part of the mega-deal he signed with them as a player prior to the 2012 season as a player.

Other known candidates for the Astros manager job are Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta and Yankees bench coach (not to mention former Tigers and Angels manager) Brad Ausmus. Former Astros third baseman Morgan Ensberg, the manager of the Triple-A Rays affiliate Durham Bulls, will also interview this week, according to MLB.com.

The Orioles are willing to listen to trade offers on any player other than Pete Alonso as they seek both rotation and outfield help, according to The Baltimore Banner. The  Orioles reportedly aren't "actively shopping" any players, but they are looking for upgrades at starting pitcher and outfielder and realize one of the ways that could happen is via a trade.

Surely they wouldn't sell low on Gunnar Henderson, given his immense upside, so we can probably take him off the table unless some team makes it worth their while. There is a glut of infielders, though. With Alonso at first base and Henderson at short, they have Jackson Holliday, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Jordan Westburg and Coby Mayo for two spots. Even using one of the four at designated hitter, it's easy to see where a deal could happen.

Westburg and Encarnacion-Strand are under team control through 2029 while Holliday is controlled through 2030 and Mayo through 2031.

The American League champion Rays recently picked up the $20 million club option on All-Star starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen. That would be a franchise-record salary for one player in a single season. It might seem odd to exercise an option and then deal a player to an outsider, but locking Rasmussen in for a one-year deal makes him an attractive trade candidate instead of just letting him walk in free agency, and this is how the Rays generally operate. We've seen it so many times: they get ahead of losing guys to free agency, sometimes even dealing them a year or two earlier. They've done it with Randy Arozarena, Isaac Paredes, Tyler Glasnow and even going back to franchise legends like David Price, Evan Longoria and Ben Zobrist.

The Rays right now are saying they intend to keep Rasmussen for 2027.

"Not a declarative this, that, whatever, but I can sit here very confidently and say that every intention right now is thinking about Ras anchoring our rotation and how to make this team better going into next year," club president Erik Neander said on Tuesday, via the Tampa Bay Times.

If they want to contend again next year, it sure seems like they need Rasmussen, with Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta off to free agency. That leaves Rasmussen atop the rotation, followed by Shane McClanahan, Griffin Jax, Ryan Pepiot and a bunch of question marks. There are questions attached to McClanahan, Jax and Pepiot too.

#2633. College football Week 11 what to watch: It's the last stand for LSU's playoff hopes in Lane Kiffin's first season

The sprint to the finish of the 2026 college football regular season is here.

Week 11 features five games between teams in the top 25 of the College Football Playoff rankings and a host of other games between ranked teams and opponents who aren't that far outside the rankings. Here's what you need to know ahead of Saturday's slate.

We were surprised to see the Blue Devils unranked in Tuesday night's CFP rankings.

Yes, Duke's two losses are to Georgia Tech and North Carolina, and yes, their last two games were against Boston College and NC State. But two wins by a combined score of 88-5 is impressive, no matter who the opponents are.

There are only two power conference teams who are 7-2 and unranked in the CFP's rankings. Both are in the ACC. SMU is also 7-2.

Saturday's game is the chance for more college football fans to learn about Nate Sheppard's greatness. The Duke running back has 191 carries for 1,189 yards and 17 scores. And there are still three games to go in the regular season. After four consecutive games with fewer than 100 yards, Sheppard had 18 carries for 217 yards and three touchdowns against NC State. He has eight rushing TDs over the past two games.

Miami is looking to rebound after its loss to Notre Dame. It took a while for Cooper Barkate and Elija Lofton to emerge against the Fighting Irish as Darian Mensah had his worst passing game of the season. Can the Hurricanes lean into the run game more than they did against Notre Dame? Javian Mallory had just three carries for 14 yards, while Mark Fletcher rushed 13 times for 57 yards.

If Miami gets the win, the Hurricanes can be on the brink of the ACC title game. Duke would have a third ACC loss and Wake Forest will either have two losses or SMU will have a third conference loss.

Can USC do something it's never done in Lincoln Riley's time with the Trojans?

Riley's USC teams have never beaten a ranked opponent on the road outside of Los Angeles. Over Riley's four-plus seasons in LA, the only win over a ranked opponent on the road came in 2022, when USC beat then-No. 16 UCLA 48-45 at the Rose Bowl. Outside of those games, USC is 0-7 as the visiting team against a team in the AP Top 25.

Both the Trojans and Hoosiers are coming off bye weeks. Week 10 was USC's second of the season after it played in Week Zero. Through three trips to the Central and Eastern Time zones this season, USC is 2-1 with one-score wins over Rutgers and Penn State, and an ugly 24-7 loss at Wisconsin.

Of course, USC rebounded after that Wisconsin game to take down Ohio State and immediately jump back into the top 25. Big plays fueled that win and it's unlikely that USC can count on replicating that formula against an Indiana defense that's been one of the best in the country — and can rush the passer better than Ohio State has this season.

The Hoosiers could start QB Grant Wilson after he took over in the second half for a banged-up Josh Hoover in the overtime win over Minnesota. No matter who starts at quarterback, we expect Indiana to try to overpower a USC defense that's giving up nearly 125 yards a game on the ground. Indiana's run game is still one of the best in the country despite the struggles through the air.

Could the Big 12 title race get thrown into chaos on Saturday night? Wins by Arizona and Oklahoma State could put a huge wrench in a potential Utah vs. Texas Tech matchup in Arlington.

As it stands entering Saturday, Utah is atop the conference with a 6-0 record, while Texas Tech is 5-1. After them, there are five teams at 4-2: BYU, Houston, Arizona, Baylor and Oklahoma State. That group could increase to six, and all of them could be just a game back of the Utes.

How much of a letdown spot is this game for the Utes, who have taken down two ranked opponents and a Cincinnati team fresh off a win over the Red Raiders across the last three weeks? In the biggest Holy War to date, Utah jumped out to a big lead and then needed to come back from a BYU comeback to beat the Cougars 28-20.

A win over Arizona and a strong game from QB Devon Dampier can vault him into the Heisman conversation. Dampier has thrown for 20 scores and run for seven others while completing 68% of his passes.

After a loss at Texas Tech, Arizona needed some late-game wildness to overcome an eight-point deficit in the fourth quarter to beat TCU 29-28. The Wildcats are still dangerous, and Noah Fifita could be the best quarterback the Utes have played all season. He's completing 73% of his passes and has thrown for over 300 yards in each of Arizona's past four games.

LSU's playoff hopes are officially gone with a loss to the Longhorns, while Texas appears to be able to withstand a defeat and still make the postseason.

Texas moved up a spot to No. 6 after beating Missouri and the Tigers remained in the CFP's rankings. That's significant, as Texas can now boast four wins over teams in this week's top 25. A fifth win Saturday night almost assures Texas of a playoff spot even if the Longhorns lose to either Arkansas or Texas A&M over the final two weeks of the season.

LSU, meanwhile, is on the brink of missing the playoff in Lane Kiffin's first season and, if you really want to be pessimistic, is closer to 7-5 than it is to making the postseason. We're fascinated to see how aggressive Kiffin is against a very good Texas defense after his fourth-down failures against Alabama. LSU was 0-of-4 on fourth-down attempts in the loss to the Crimson Tide. Will he be dissuaded, especially if he faces an early fourth-down decision?

The Longhorns could have Cam Coleman back after he sat out the Missouri game and should have a healthier Colin Simmons. The star edge rusher tried to give it a go in his first game back from an ankle injury, but ended up sitting out the second half against Mizzou. No opposing offense has averaged over 6 yards a play against LSU all season, and none of the Tigers' last three opponents have accumulated over 300 yards.

Yet LSU has also forced just one turnover in that span. The Tigers may need a couple from Arch Manning to get the win.

We're prepared for a second straight Texas Tech game to have over 100 total points.

In Week 10, Texas Tech took down West Virginia 53-48 thanks to a late safety on a sack of Mountaineers QB Michael Hawkins. Oklahoma State, meanwhile, had 49 points in the first half as it beat Kansas State 66-28.

This is not the Texas Tech defense we watched a year ago. While Jacob Rodriguez finished fifth in the Heisman voting and Tech allowed 11.8 points per game last year, the Red Raiders are giving up 24 points per game and 5.6 yards a play in 2026. Tech ranks 65th in opponent points per game.

Former Florida State and Boston College QB Thomas Castellanos has rushed for over 100 yards in each of his two starts since taking over for Will Hammond as Texas Tech's quarterback. Castellanos rushed 23 times for 102 yards and threw for 362 yards and five touchdowns against WVU.

The OSU defense is better than West Virginia's — though that's damning with faint praise. Oklahoma State is 93rd in the country in scoring defense at 27.2 points per game. But if it can slow Castellanos and RB J'Koby Williams down enough, OSU's offense can take advantage.

QB Drew Mestemaker is sneaking up the Heisman odds and has thrown for 29 TDs and nearly 3,000 yards. RB Caleb Hawkins has rushed for 1,081 yards and has added 424 yards receiving. Both WR Wyatt Young and WR Justin Bowick have over 750 receiving yards.

Since scoring just 10 points in Week 1 against Tulsa, Oklahoma State hasn't scored fewer than 32 over its last eight games. Texas Tech has given up at least 25 points in its last four games. The ingredients are very much there for a shootout.

No. 13 Wake Forest at SMU (-1.5) (Noon ET, ESPN): A win for Wake Forest puts the Demon Deacons in prime position for the ACC title game ahead of games vs. Georgia Tech and Duke. SMU isn't out of the ACC title picture either, and has No. 5 Notre Dame in Week 12. The Mustangs bounced back from a Halloween loss at Syracuse with a dominating Friday night win over Virginia Tech in Week 10.

Northwestern at No. 20 Ohio State (-12.5) (Noon ET, Fox): You have to go back to the 2011 season when Ohio State finished 6-7 to find the Buckeyes' last three-game losing streak. Northwestern's Aidan Chiles missed the Wildcats' loss to Iowa and his presence may be paramount to Northwestern's hopes of an upset. Northwestern had just 286 yards of offense on 69 plays against the Hawkeyes.

No. 8 Tennessee (-2.5) at Texas A&M (3 p.m. ET, ESPN): Yes, Texas A&M is just 1-5 in SEC play and still less than a field goal underdog to a top-10 opponent. That's how the SEC has gone this year. It wouldn't be surprising in the slightest to see the Aggies get the win as Tennessee is coming off a huge home win over Kentucky.

No. 22 Missouri at No. 1 Georgia (-15.5) (3:30 p.m. ET, ABC): The Tigers were still somehow ranked after losing at home to Texas and need wins over Georgia, Kentucky and Oklahoma to even have a hope of making the College Football Playoff. Georgia looks like the clear top team in the conference after its demolition of Ole Miss following an easy win over Florida.

Florida at No. 11 Kentucky (-3.5) (6:15 p.m. ET, ESPN): The Wildcats are the last team provisionally in the playoff after their loss to the Volunteers. Florida, meanwhile, has lost four of its last five games after a 4-0 start. The Wildcats have won the last three matchups against the Gators in Lexington, including a 38-7 win in 2025.

#2630. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

Here's how the preliminary lottery odds look for those 16 teams in the mix, based on how they finished the 2026 season:

It's too soon to know which players will be in the mix for that top pick since the amateur seasons haven't begun yet. However, two early favorites to go No. 1 are University of Florida shortstop Brendan Lawson and Mississippi State left-hander Tomas Valinicius.

Gustav Isaksen sente la fiducia di Gattuso. L’esterno della Lazio, in ritiro con la Danimarca per le sfide di Nations League, descrive così il rapporto con il tecnico: «Sento la fiducia di Gattuso! #2627. NBA relegation zone predictions: Ranking the 7 worst teams in the race to avoid the bottom of the standings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When the NBA reformed the draft lottery, it did so with the hopes that all 30 teams would be somewhat competitive. But two weeks into the 2026-27 season, that isn't proving true.

Five teams have just a single win so far this season, and in many cases, those wins are only coming when they play one another. The Los Angeles Clippers have only beaten the Sacramento Kings. The Chicago Bulls have only beaten the Milwaukee Bucks. The Kings' only win came when the Dallas Mavericks rested Kyrie Irving.

No matter how the incentive structures are designed, the NBA will always have a handful of very bad teams. Some teams are poorly run. Some teams are besieged by injuries. Some teams are simply in transitional stages of their roster builds. The old NBA was designed to make bad teams good quickly. The new one is designed to make it harder for teams to bounce back from the bottom.

As part of last spring's lottery reform, the three worst teams in the league are now punished for losing. In the new 3-2-1 lottery format, the seven best teams to miss the Play-In Tournament get three lottery balls each out of the 37 available ones, while the three worst teams each get only two. In theory, that should create an all-out war to avoid the bottom three. In practice, well, we'll get into that shortly.

For now, as the bottom of the league is starting to take shape, let's take a look at our relegation zone candidates. While injuries could certainly create more of them as we go, seven teams stand out as reasonable threats for a bottom-three record so far this season. We're going to rank them from least to most likely to land in the relegation zone, with the top three teams being our official picks to take that lottery hit in May.

Remember, this is not merely a ranking of the NBA's worst teams. It's who is likeliest to land in the bottom three of the standings, a necessary distinction for reasons you're about to find out.

There isn't a more dumbfounding team to watch in the NBA right now than the Jazz. For four years, Utah was a smart, well-run team that lost because the front office did everything in its power to deprive its coach of talent. Well, coach Will Hardy is allowed to win now. It just isn't happening.

The inventive, flowing offense of years past is sputtering. No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson isn't making jumpers and can't get to the rim. Players needed for size and defense -- like Josh Okogie and Jaxson Hayes -- are killing the offense. Everything is running through Keyonte George because he's the only player on the floor creating consistent advantages. He's not a true point guard, and the lack of passing on the floor right now is palpable. Their lone victory came by a single point at home against the New Orleans Pelicans. Not exactly inspiring.

Any dreams of a 50-win, top-six seed season died with the Walker Kessler trade. This team is screaming for anyone who can screen and rebound. Getting Jusuf Nurkić back will help, and eventually, Jaren Jackson Jr. will take the floor again, too. You'd hope Peterson eventually figures some things out. He's a No. 2 overall pick. He's too talented to struggle this much unless the medical issues that plagued him at Kansas are persisting. There are reasons to believe this will get better. The Jazz should eventually be at least competitive.

But we're barely into November and even their more modest, post-Kessler Play-In ambitions already seem to be on life support. The Western Conference is far deeper than it looked a month ago and the Jazz are digging themselves a hole they're going to struggle to climb out of. This is a bad defensive roster even at full strength, and if the offense is this disjointed, the postseason just isn't on the table. After a four-year tank, that's a real concern in Utah. Even sniffing the relegation zone, given the time spent even getting to this point, is a borderline disaster.

The Suns come in ahead of one-win Utah -- and the two-win Orlando Magic they just beat -- because those teams have more substantial reinforcements incoming. The Suns will benefit greatly from the eventual return of Mark Williams, if only because, at this stage, Khaman Maluach just is not ready to play serious NBA minutes. But Williams isn't, say, Jaren Jackson or Paolo Banchero. Phoenix's problems are internal.

They were the first team of the season to leak displeasure to the press, with Chris Haynes reporting that the locker room is frustrated over the lack of a point guard. There's a fair bit of statistical evidence suggesting the Suns could address that problem by benching Jalen Green for Collin Gillespie. Eventually, Green's performance will force the issue. If your value is derived entirely from scoring and you're averaging 12 points on 41-22-69 shooting splits, you won't be long for anyone's starting lineup.

The bigger problem here is the loss of last year's defense-and-hustle identity. The Suns only just surrendered the NBA's 30th defensive ranking to another team on this list, and their deflections, loose ball recoveries and offensive rebounding are way down. As of this writing, they're the worst rebounding team in the NBA. Many of the players responsible for last year's identity are playing less than they did last year. Green simply isn't a defense and energy player. Neither is Miles Bridges, who they gave up yet another unprotected first-round pick to get.

Devin Booker is slipping. The shotmaking bar on superstar-level value for a guard who never makes plays nor gets to the rim at an elite level is almost impossibly high. He basically has to be a high-volume 3-point shooter making close to 40% of his attempts to justify his supermax deal. He hasn't come close to that in years. He doesn't quite have his old burst, either, and after the Bridges trade, the Suns are down to very few remaining draft assets with which they can improve. There's probably enough talent here that the Suns will eventually be able to eke their way to 30 or so wins, but the early returns here are pretty discouraging.

Here's where we take our first real step down in terms of roster talent. The bottom five teams are simply worse than the remaining 25. There's no All Star-level talent here, like George in Utah or Booker in Phoenix. Michael Porter Jr. made his case a year ago, but his volume is down with Julius Randle on the roster. With the Nets, Randle has been largely inefficient and is turning the ball over more than ever. Only three teams turn the ball over more frequently than they do.

They're attempting to sacrifice high opponent 3-point volume for minimizing attempts at the rim. It's working in terms of volume, but once anyone does get to the rim, they're scoring there with impunity because Brooklyn simply doesn't have a reliable, individual rim protector. They're among the most frequent fouling defenses in the NBA. Last year's No. 8 overall pick, Egor Dëmin, is already hurt and has all but abandoned shooting inside the arc. Young guards, no matter how much promise they show, are usually bad. The goal of this season is to develop several of them. Mikel Brown Jr. and the improving Nolan Traore are years away from what they'll eventually become.

Here's where we really have to start talking about incentives. Brooklyn owes its first-round pick to the Houston Rockets. Now, the Jazz and Suns owe their first-round picks out as well, but under different circumstances. The Suns won't control their own pick again until the actual sun burns out, so what happens to their picks isn't really their concern. The Jazz have picked in the top five two years in a row, so their pick, currently owed to the Memphis Grizzlies, can't land there again, and will therefore have a clean slate next year. But the Nets, who are several years away from winning meaningfully barring something unforeseen, probably want to avoid having their pick land in the top five, as teams are forbidden from ending up there three years in a row, or, in the worst-case scenario, coming in at No. 1, which would bar them from picking there in 2028.

The Nets are, in other words, incentivized to lose, which is exactly what this system was supposed to prevent. Now, they can't go about it as brazenly as tankers of the past have, as commissioner Adam Silver now has expanded powers to punish teams for tanking. But the NBA can't stop them from, say, trading useful veterans like Porter at the deadline. Brooklyn didn't do so a year ago when it should have, so this will be something to watch when February rolls around. If the Nets keep Porter, they're probably good enough to duck the relegation zone. If they move him, well, getting in there may not be the goal, but it would be a potentially helpful byproduct.

Considering the Nets traded for Randle in June, though, it seems as though Brooklyn, to the delight of Houston (which walks away with six lottery balls between Brooklyn and Phoenix in this scenario), intends to try to win. There are possible reasons for that ranging from culture-building to job security, but until the Nets show their hand, we'll leave them out of the bottom three for now.

Here's a sobering thought: of the seven teams we're covering in this space, the Kings are the only one that fits into the relegation zone system as intended. They don't owe their pick out to another team. They aren't on any consecutive high picks clock. They're just a bad team trying to rebuild organically. They want high draft picks, which means they don't want to be in the bottom three.

They might even be willing to trade a small asset to improve at the deadline for this purpose if necessary. If nothing else, they have the salary to do so. Between Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter, they have over $70 million in expiring money to dangle if doing so makes sense. Wins tend to be elusive in Sacramento, but the Kings actually want them.

They are unfortunately ill-equipped to get them. The 2026-27 Kings are quite frankly one of the strangest teams ever assembled. Former All-Star Domantas Sabonis is playing 36 minutes a game and attempting fewer shots than Precious Achiuwa. Darius Acuff Jr., meanwhile, has the second-highest usage rate any rookie has posted in NBA history, behind only Joel Embiid. He has higher usage this season than Cade Cunningham and Jalen Brunson.

The Kings aren't playing like a team whose goal is to win. They are playing like a team whose sole goal is to fast-forward through Acuff's developmental curve. That's not a crazy decision given their circumstances, but as we've addressed with Brooklyn, young guards can be productive without being especially helpful when it comes to winning. Acuff is taking shots that players like Brunson and Cunningham spend whole careers earning the right to attempt, and he is understandably far worse at actually converting them. Veteran teammates don't tend to enjoy watching rookies chuck bad shots, and without a good defender in sight, it's not as though the Kings can win on the other end of the floor. They're going to be on the bubble here. We just have three better candidates.

The ball-handling deficit here is bleak. Only the Charlotte Hornets are turning the ball over more, and nobody is even close when it comes to points allowed off turnovers. Considering Darius Garland's perpetual issues staying on the court, things are only going to get harder from here. Getting Brandon Ingram back from his partially torn Achilles will help, but he's much more of an individual shotmaker than someone who can lift an entire offense. They're struggling to generate anything near the rim as well, ranking 24th in paint points thus far. They're defending better than most of this group, a byproduct of Jeff Van Gundy's presence on their bench, but even that is at risk because of those pesky incentive structures.

The Clippers obviously owe their own first-round pick to the Oklahoma City Thunder. That isn't especially relevant, but we should note that the Clippers owe their top-three protected pick to the Philadelphia 76ers in 2029 through swap rights, and they'd probably prefer to avoid starting that top-five clock now because consecutive top-five picks would ensure they have no chance of keeping their 2029 selection.

More importantly, though, the Clippers were just stripped of five first-round picks for circumventing the salary cap. That puts them at an enormous draft capital deficit moving forward. There's no way the Clippers can recoup all of that lost value, but it makes plenty of sense for them to trade veterans for whatever value they can get in the name of setting up their future. Players like Brook Lopez, Kris Dunn, Max Strus, Derrick Jones Jr. and Rui Hachimura are all in their primes and could net positive value back in the right trades.

Since the Clippers have nothing to lose by getting relegated this year, it would likely behoove them to cash in these players for whatever value they get. If they do so, they're going to wind up in pretty rough shape down the stretch.

From a team we know circumvented the cap to a team we think very well might have. The Bucks are currently being investigated for the contract they gave Gary Trent Jr. over the summer. And the fact that he has now been DNP-CD'd in six of Milwaukee's eight games certainly doesn't help their case. If they lose picks, they're incentivized to try to make those up by trading away players they don't intend to keep long-term.

Even as it stands, the Bucks are just a bad team. They're a bottom-five offense and defense with no notable injuries. The roster mix is what you'd expect out of a team that just traded the best player in franchise history without receiving a premium asset in return: a jumbled mess. Half of the roster is comprised of shooting guards. They're thin enough at forward that they're still forced to start Kyle Kuzma, and their $108 million starting center, Myles Turner, is averaging single digits. The young players are years away. The old players are years away from the versions of themselves that warranted the minutes and money they're currently receiving.

None of this is especially surprising. It's the first year of a rebuild, and the Bucks won't control their own pick again until 2031. They're in no rush here, and the Pelicans, who control Milwaukee's pick this year, stand to lose draft value because of it.

The Bulls have been the NBA's worst team this season by a pretty comfortable margin. A brutal early schedule is somewhat to blame, of course, but they have nearly a five-point net rating gap between themselves and the No. 29-ranked Kings. They're a bottom-five defense in terms of both points in the paint allowed per game and 3-pointers made per game.

Only the Clippers give up more points off of turnovers. They rank 27th in rebounding rate. Years of steady scoring growth from Josh Giddey have seemingly been undone in two weeks. Matas Buzelis is both playing and shooting less than he did a year ago. Caleb Wilson is exploring the studio space in all of the messy ways you want a top rookie to do so. They're shooting just over 27% from 3-point range.

So the Bulls have the basketball end of the equation covered... but they also have the incentive side to consider. Remember, Wilson was the No. 4 overall pick in June. That means that another top-five pick in 2027 locks them out of the top five in 2028. The 2027 class is considered historically weak, but 2028 is expected to be stronger. Realistically, the Bulls probably don't expect to be any good next year, either. The last thing they should want is to risk getting stuck with a middling 2028 pick because they land at No. 5 in 2027.

Chicago is already terrible and has good reason to try to stay that way. Wilson has an incredibly bright future, but the present is understandably bleak.
