#2607. NFL trade deadline: Ranking all 18 in-season deals as Kirk Cousins, Jeffery Simmons reshape Super Bowl race

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The fourth-most active trade deadline in NFL history is complete. Teams completed 18 in-season moves by the time the clock struck 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday as they positioned themselves for postseason runs and rebuilds. The biggest blockbusters that defined the deadline sent star defensive tackles to Super Bowl contenders and quarterback help to sputtering offenses, and those should prove with time to be the most impactful deals of the year.

Some moves that occurred well in advance of the deadline have already paid dividends. Jeffery Simmons, for instance, is already a difference-maker for the Chicago Bears and was integral in their building a four-game winning streak. Others delivered mixed results, as is the case with the Quenton Nelson and Joey Porter Jr. deals since both players are dealing with injuries early in their tenures with the Seattle Seahawks and Dallas Cowboys, respectively. As for those that flew in just ahead of the deadline, the next few weeks will determine which teams won or lost their trades.

Trades are about more than just coming away with more talent than the other team involved. Evaluating the impact of a transaction comes down to specific team needs, the capital sent back in return and how the move addresses short-term contention prospects and long-term roster outlooks.

With those factors in mind, below are all 18 in-season trades ranked from most to least impactful.

There was one missing piece in Minnesota that, if found, could turn the Vikings into a force to be reckoned with in the Super Bowl race. It took until the last minute, but they found it. Kirk Cousins promises to give the Vikings the offensive lift they need to capitalize on their league-best defense. This year has been a renaissance for the 38-year-old who is on pace to threaten for his first 40-touchdown season. That late-career surge and his familiarity with the offense in Minnesota should allow him to step right into action and help the Vikings avoid the tight, low-scoring battles of the campaign's first nine weeks and start blowing opponents out. His arrival ought to also unlock Justin Jefferson and turn him back into the superstar-level producer he is meant to be.

There is a strong case to be made that Jeffery Simmons is the best in-season acquisition, because he already proved to be a game-changer for the Bears. The impacts of the other trade deadline moves are speculative, while Simmons' is known. He wreaked all kinds of havoc over his first two games in the middle of the Chicago defensive line, was paramount in the Bears' win over the Seahawks and was one of the few reasons why they survived their five-turnover disaster on "Sunday Night Football" in Week 9. The three-time All-Pro turned the defense into a significant asset overnight. That is a transformational impact that will help this team maximize its potential with Caleb Williams leading the charge on the other side of the ball.

The Jaguars were one of just two teams to trade a first-round pick. They also packaged a 2029 second-rounder to land Jordan Davis. It was a high price, but that was to be expected, since Davis is a franchise-building block who signed a contract extension with the Eagles earlier this year and will be under team control for three years beyond this one. The trade should pay dividends both straight away and over the long term as the Jaguars step into their championship-contention window. It was about as big of a swing as Jacksonville could have made in the wake of the torn quad that knocked DaVon Hamilton out for the year. They did not just replace Hamilton; they upgraded.

The impact Jessie Bates III delivers to the Jaguars' defense in 2026 might be even greater than that of Davis, but he checks in one spot lower in the rankings because of the potential short-term nature of his stay in Jacksonville. The star safety is in the final year of his contract and may turn out to be a rental. If that is all he is, then the secondary will enjoy every minute of his half season in town, because as a three-time All-Pro, there are few defensive backfield stalwarts as talented as he is. Bates elevates the starting lineup but also minimizes the impact of losing Eric Murray for the season due to an elbow issue. Pass defense has been one of the few knocks against the otherwise elite Jaguars, as they rank 22nd in slowing teams down through the air. This helps immensely in that regard.

Amani Hooker is tied for the league lead in interceptions and already has five takeaways for the second time in three years. That kind of turnover prowess in the defensive backfield through 2028 is worth spending a second-round pick and a fifth-round pick. The Titans captain has allowed a passer rating of just 79.3 this season, which is his best mark since his rookie season in 2019. For a Bills team that scores at will and just needs its defense to hold up its end of the bargain, Hooker's arrival raises the floor and the ceiling. Safety was a need after the Bills released C.J. Gardner-Johnson, and they filled it in an emphatic way.

The 49ers' reunion with DeForest Buckner addressed a serious deficiency on the defensive line, where injuries once again reared their ugly heads. Alfred Collins and CJ West remain on injured reserve, and Gracen Halton just suffered a season-ending ankle fracture in Buckner's first game back in the Bay Area. San Francisco can seemingly never have enough playmakers amid its never-ending injury woes. Bringing Buckner back was more than just insurance, though. It is a step up in the trenches, which will aid the NFC West leaders as they pursue a championship.

Jaxson Dart's season is over, but the Giants' campaign is far from done. Even though the J.J. McCarthy trade did not make all the sense in the world when it happened, it has aged phenomenally, with the third-year quarterback stepping up as a commendable replacement for the injured starter. McCarthy is 2-0 as a starter and is playing the best football of his career (albeit in a small sample size) and has done nothing but keep the Giants comfortably in first place in the NFC East. This is not a long-term answer for New York since Dart will reclaim the No. 1 job next year, but if it allows the Giants to win the division and flip McCarthy -- or keep him as a renowned backup -- then it is a massive victory in the face of unfortunate circumstances.

The jury is out on whether Jacoby Brissett can keep the Ravens afloat until Lamar Jackson returns from thumb surgery. On one hand, he has been a premier backup for years and should be far more capable of directing the ball in the way of Zay Flowers and Derrick Henry than Joe Fagnano was in his spot start. But on the other hand, the Cardinals benched him before they moved on from him. This was a desperation trade for the Ravens that, if it pays off, will result in them remaining on the fringes of postseason contention. If Brissett is nothing more than a bottom-tier starter, though, Baltimore can kiss this season goodbye.

Quenton Nelson underwent a minor knee procedure to remove loose bodies in his knee, which is a hiccup in his young Seahawks tenure and slightly downgrades the value of the trade. The expectation should be for Nelson to return within a couple of weeks and play at an All-Pro level. But he did not impress in his debut in Seattle, will miss at least some time, and is set to become a free agent at the end of the year, so the amount of time he spends making a real impact in the trenches could be slim when it is all said and done. The Seahawks need his supreme blocking ability in the lineup to help jump-start their dormant run game.

When he is on the field, Joey Porter Jr. is a lockdown corner for the Cowboys. But he missed his first game upon arrival in Dallas with an illness and missed time over the last two weeks with an ankle issue, and it is not as if the middling defense was all that much better overall in the four games he did play to date. Unless Jerry Jones re-signs Porter in the offseason -- and that seems like a stretch given Porter's demands and Jones' typical unwillingness to pay a premium to keep free agents -- this will be a rental situation. A rental with trouble staying on the field. It looks clear that the Cowboys were more than just a standout cornerback away from figuring things out on defense.

Kansas City would have had no excuse for coming away from the trade deadline without a wide receiver. Chiefs wideouts account for just 46.0% of the team's receiving yards, which is the second-lowest rate in the NFL. Josh Downs could help take some of the pressure off the tight end group and running back Kenneth Walker III in the receiving department and perhaps free up Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy to become greater big-play threats. In order for the Chiefs to truly be back to their Super Bowl-contending ways, they have to be more balanced on offense. Downs' arrival, at the very least, will not hurt in their quest for more passing production.

The Ravens were in a tough spot at center when Tyler Linderbaum left in free agency and found their answer in early October when they made a play for Cam Jurgens, a two-time Pro Bowler and a Super Bowl champion who was part of the Eagles' legendary run at offensive line. Early returns on the trade are underwhelming, though. Jurgens is already up to 16 pressures allowed this year and was hit with multiple penalties in the early going, which is no recipe for success in an offense that has churned through quarterbacks behind him. Some of the troubles can be chalked up to the underwhelming guard play next to him, though.

A rash of injuries devastated San Francisco's wide receiver group over the first half of the season and emphasized the need for even more bodies in what went from a deep group to a thin one in short order. When Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel Sr. are healthy, Keenan Allen projects as an ideal third option for MVP-contending quarterback Brock Purdy. He was the top-producing receiver in Indianapolis on a per-game basis, so he clearly still has something to give in the latter stages of his career. Expect Allen to command a sizable role in the immediate future before potentially giving way to De'Zhaun Stribling when he returns from injured reserve and serving as a depth piece and ready-made starter when his number is called.

When the Texans took a shot on Marvin Harrison Jr., it made all the sense in the world. Their wide receiver group needed a No. 2 receiver to step up; the Cardinals were clearly out on him as part of their future, and he has tons of experience working with C.J. Stroud dating back to their time together at Ohio State. There is still time for him to turn his career around, especially since he remains under contract through 2028. But even with a touchdown in one of his first three games in Houston, Harrison has done little to command a consistent role. The Texans may have given up a second-round pick and a fifth-rounder for someone who will remain behind Nico Collins, Xavier Hutchinson, Kayshon Boutte, Jaylin Noel and Tank Dell in the pecking order.

The Broncos should feel great about taking a starting inside linebacker away from a division rival, even if it came at the cost of two draft picks. Daiyan Henley projects to step back from his starting job with the Chargers and assume a rotational role behind Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad, so he will be a premier second-string option at the position on an already stout defense. This is the kind of move that will fly under the radar so long as Henley plays off the bench, but one that makes a rich unit even richer and gives Denver meaningful depth on the road to a deep playoff run.

The NFL's worst pass defense is a little less bleak now than it was before the Andre Cisco trade, but the move might not move the needle enough to make a meaningful difference in the Lions' inability to keep opponents off the field. Cisco can step into the lineup next to Brian Branch, but this has the look of more of a depth addition as Detroit awaits the return of Kerby Joseph. The latter's insertion back into action will do far more to improve upon the Lions' 260.9 passing yards allowed per game than Cisco. Joseph will either be activated by Nov. 17 or shut down for the rest of the year. In that sense, the Cisco move makes plenty of sense. But the Lions would, of course, prefer not to rely on him as a starter.

Had the Jaguars stopped at the Davon Godchaux trade, they would have plugged a hole on their defensive line with a space-eating run stopper and pulled off a one-for-one replacement for the injured DaVon Hamilton. Of course, they proceeded to land Davis hours later, thus reducing the importance of the Godchaux deal. In the end, this comes out as a depth addition on a defensive line that is in flux but one that should be among the league's best at defending the run. Jacksonville is in a tremendous spot as it surges toward the No. 1 seed in the AFC.

It came as a surprise to see the Ravens make a last-minute move for another center, since they had already acquired one in Jurgens just over a month ago, but they landed Ryan Neuzil and pried him away from his starting job with the Falcons. Neuzil has ample experience at guard, so he could shift over to the left side of the line and replace John Simpson. He may also become the team's top reserve on the interior and one capable of playing at either guard spot or at center should he be thrust into action. Time will tell how the Ravens deploy him, and until then, the grade on the deal is incomplete.

#2604. MLB rumors: Tarik Skubal's market already hot, contenders eyeing Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. Skubal is expected to sign in November, before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, though a deal is not imminent. Talks are underway, however, and his market is moving.

Skubal is expected to sign a record contract at least in total value, and possibly in average annual value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract ever given out. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander's matching $43.3 million salaries with the Mets years ago set the record for the average annual value for a pitcher.

The Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, and Yankees are among the teams linked to Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports the New York Post. Unless MLB and the MLBPA unexpectedly avoid a lockout, Sato must sign before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Otherwise, he will return to the Hanshin Tigers for 2027.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. He has significant power but also swing-and-miss and defensive concerns at third base, similar to Munetaka Murakami a year ago. Murakami slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games as a rookie this season, providing proof of concept for Sato.

The Nationals have signed center fielder Jacob Young to a four-year extension, reports FanSided. The deal is worth $23 million and includes an $8 million club option for a fifth year. The extension buys out Young's three arbitration years and one free agent year, with a club option for a second free agent year. He's now under Washington's control through 2031.

Young, 27, has always been a superlative defender. He unlocked a new level on offense this season, particularly in the second half, when he hit .301 with a .385 on-base percentage. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.

#2603. NFL pretenders and contenders after Week 9: NFC North is fierce, no faith in Giants and Steelers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Now that we are halfway through the 2026 NFL season, it's time to start paying attention to the playoff picture -- and it's a pretty wild picture to look at right now.

The NFC North is the only division to ever feature four teams three or more games above .500 through Week 9, while the NFC South is the only division to feature four teams two or more games below .500. Is every NFC North team going to make the playoffs? And which NFC South team will likely go one-and-done in the postseason?

Below, we will break down the pretenders and contenders in the NFL right now. We will look at the 14 teams that would make the playoffs if the season ended today, and examine if they have a legitimate shot to hoist the Lombardi Trophy. Let's begin with the contenders.

The 7-1 Buffalo Bills are off to their best eight-game start to a season since 1993, which was when they made their last Super Bowl appearance. Josh Allen is again an MVP favorite, James Cook has rushed for at least 75 yards and a touchdown in seven straight games, and Jim Leonhard's defense left the Minnesota Vikings front office scrambling after Carson Wentz registered one of the worst quarterback showings in franchise history on Monday night. The Bills are again a contender.

The San Francisco 49ers are your Super Bowl favorites right now over at DraftKings Sportsbook (+540), and it's easy to understand why. They have started 7-1 or better for the first time since 2019, when they made the Super Bowl. Brock Purdy is an MVP favorite, and he leads an offense that is averaging 29.4 points per game -- which ranks No. 3 in the NFL. This past week against the Las Vegas Raiders, the 49ers scored two passing touchdowns, two rushing touchdowns and a defensive touchdown. However, health will again be a major talking point when it comes to San Francisco. Wide receivers Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel are still sidelined, and defensive tackle Gracen Halton suffered a broken ankle on Sunday. If they can return some players for the stretch run, this could be the 49ers' year.

The Denver Broncos have been dancing with the devil all season in these one-score games, but I'll remind you Bo Nix and Co. did the same thing last year, and could have made the Super Bowl if Nix didn't suffer that ankle injury in the divisional round. The Broncos have won five straight games since their 2-2 start, and while they have the worst yard differential (-699) by any team that started 7-2 or better in NFL history, all Nix has done is step up in crunch time. He's 18-12 in his career when trailing in the second half, and 13-12 when trailing in the fourth quarter. Those are the best win percentages by any quarterback since 1970, with a minimum of 20 games. Defensively, Denver is giving up more yards per game than last year, but still ranks top 10 in scoring with 20.7 points allowed per game. You could make the case that the Broncos are pretenders, but I'm leaning the other way. They beat Josh Allen and the Bills in the playoffs last year, and have already defeated the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs this season. Denver could make the AFC Championship again.

The Jaguars are all-in this year. At the trade deadline, they sent a first-round pick, second-round pick, a future second-round pick, a future fifth-round pick and a conditional sixth-round pick for defensive tackle Jordan Davis, defensive tackle Davon Godchaux and safety Jessie Bates III. Giving up first- and second-round picks for Davis was shocking, but there's no doubt the Jaguars roster got better this week.

The Jags are running away with the AFC South at 6-2, and have as many wins as the rest of their rivals combined. They are 14-2 in their past 16 games dating back to last year, and Trevor Lawrence has statistically been the best quarterback during that stretch with 42 total touchdowns and a 108.8 passer rating. The Jaguars have the second-best scoring defense in the NFL (15.1 points allowed per game) and one of the best run defenses in the league as well, allowing just 89.3 yards per game. Justice Hill actually just became the first running back to rush for 75 yards against the Jags in 25 games.

The Chiefs got back on track this past week against the New York Jets, registering their largest win (23 points) since Week 7 in 2025. Kenneth Walker III also got back on track with 143 total yards and three touchdowns. There's still some concern around Patrick Mahomes' passing game, but the addition of Josh Downs will be helpful. Chiefs receivers are averaging 117.5 yards per game, which ranks 28th in the NFL. That hasn't stopped Kansas City from having what is statistically the second-best offense in the NFL (384.1 yards per game).

This may be Joe Burrow's year to win MVP. He's accounted for 26 total touchdowns through eight games. Five of the previous seven players to score that many touchdowns through eight games won MVP. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins have combined for 47 receptions, 693 yards and eight touchdowns just over the last three games. We know what Chase is capable of, but Higgins is having the best year of his NFL career. He's averaging 94.8 receiving yards per game and has caught six touchdowns in eight games.

Where there's concern with the Cincinnati Bengals is their rushing attack. The 85.6 rushing yards per game are the fewest by a team to start 6-2 or better since the 2014 Detroit Lions. We'll see if the Bengals can pass their way to a Super Bowl. Cincy's defense still isn't "great" statistically, but it's much improved compared to the past couple of seasons. That in itself gives the Bengals a legitimate shot.

It's hard not to like the Chicago Bears. They have an offensive madman scheming up talented weapons open downfield, a quarterback who looks like Josh Allen, and a defense that has been sparked by the addition of Jeffery Simmons. The Bears can't turn the ball over five times every game as they did on Sunday night, but I'm not too worried about that issue.

The Bears have the firepower offensively to be a Super Bowl contender, from the rushing attack to the passing attack, and a defense that is good enough to support a playoff run. The addition of Simmons affects that unit in more ways than one. He can stuff the run and can pressure the quarterback from the interior -- which in turn makes life easier on those in the secondary.

I'm on the fence with the Lions. We all know about the offense with Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown, but the issue has always been Detroit's defense.

The reason I'll place the Lions in the "contender" category is that Kelvin Sheppard's unit has been better in recent weeks. After a disastrous start, the Lions have allowed just 15.5 points per game during this current four-game win streak. They were allowing 31.8 points per game during the 2-2 start. With Brian Branch back, hopefully Kerby Joseph soon, and the addition of Andre Cisco, I think the Lions can be a contender.

If I were power-ranking the teams in the NFC North, I would have the Green Bay Packers third or fourth. So, does that make them a contender or pretender? I'm still trying to figure that out.

The turnaround in Green Bay has been incredible. After that horrific 1-2 start, the Packers are playing better on both sides of the ball. Jordan Love is the best deep-ball thrower in the NFL, and Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are looking like Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle did in Miami during those fun Mike McDaniel years. The two have combined for 1,662 receiving yards thus far. However, like the Bengals, the Packers can't run the ball. They rank dead last in rushing offense with 68.2 yards per game, and just lost Josh Jacobs to a broken finger.

I'm not placing money on the Packers to win the Super Bowl, but I can't get over how good this passing attack has been. Plus, the defense just picked off Drake Maye three times and will return Micah Parsons soon.

The Vikings were perhaps the most obvious pretender in the NFL despite the 6-2 record. Kyler Murray's passing offense was statistically one of the worst in the NFL, as his 170.3 passing yards per game ranked 30th among 31 qualifying passers entering Week 9. When Carson Wentz replaced him in the lineup on Monday night against Buffalo, some people thought it would open up the offense a bit. Instead, Wentz registered the worst passer rating by a Vikings quarterback (8.9) in a game since 1984, while completing 32% of his passes.

However, I'm willing to entertain the possibility that the Vikings are now contenders with the addition of Kirk Cousins at the trade deadline. He's been playing good football for the Raiders, as his 20 passing touchdowns rank second in the NFL, and his 260.0 passing yards per game rank eighth. Cousins has chemistry with Justin Jefferson -- and that may be an understatement. Jefferson's 98.9 receiving yards per game when catching passes from Cousins are the most by a QB-WR duo all-time (min. 50 games). With the backing of a Brian Flores defense, the Vikings are a team to watch moving forward.

The New York Giants are the frontrunner in the NFC East, but I don't know how realistic their Super Bowl chances are. In fact, DraftKings Sportsbook believes the 3-5 Houston Texans and 3-6 Tampa Bay Buccaneers have just as good a shot at winning it all this year.

J.J. McCarthy has been better than expected at the quarterback position, but still hasn't thrown a touchdown in his two starts. In fact, he's the only quarterback in the past 40 years to win a game with zero passing touchdowns in four straight starts. New York has what is statistically a top five defense under new coordinator Dennard Wilson and Defensive Rookie of the Year favorite Arvell Reese, but there are at least five teams in the NFC I'm more confident in.

The New England Patriots were destroyed at home by the Packers on Sunday, 45-27. Those 45 points were the most allowed in a home game since 1970. Christian Gonzalez struggled to keep up with the dynamic duo of Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, while Drake Maye threw three interceptions. To make matters worse, running back Rhamondre Stevenson is reportedly dealing with a knee injury that will sideline him for a couple of weeks, while TreVeyon Henderson remains out after experiencing an "unusual medical emergency." The Patriots running backs are now Corey Kiner and Lan Larison.

Even with Mike Tomlin gone, I still view the Pittsburgh Steelers the same. A feisty team that can make the playoffs and maybe even steal the division, but is not a legitimate Super Bowl contender.

With that said, there are reasons to believe the Steelers could be a sleeper. Aaron Rodgers' offense is averaging 26.2 points per game over their last six, plus Jaylen Warren is one of the most improved players in the NFL this season. He's already up to 998 total yards in eight games played. That ranks fifth in the NFL.

Whether the Carolina Panthers win the NFC South or not, I don't view them as a Super Bowl contender. The Panthers have lost three straight games and are averaging 17.7 points per contest during this skid. Carolina's offensive line and cornerback room have been hit hard by injuries, and this team is now a +225 underdog to win the division.

#2602. Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson explains infamous 'analytically' quote during playoffs loss to Knicks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NBA players regularly draw scrutiny for things they say to the press, but coaches tend to be reserved enough to avoid getting too much egg on their faces. Kenny Atkinson is a recent exception; the Cleveland Cavaliers coach has been mocked for the past six months or so for his now-infamous comments after Game 3 of the Eastern Conference Finals.

With the Cavaliers down 3-0 to the New York Knicks, Atkinson was asked how he could give hope to his players, as no team in NBA history has ever overcome a 3-0 series deficit. "Analytically … we've won 2 out of 3," Atkinson said at the time. "We're two out of the three in the expected score. If you believe in process and all that, like, man, take that later. I don't throw that on them. I see it for myself, and if I have this feeling, I can go to our analytical table and be like, man, the expected score was like one point or two — us shooting way below expected, them shooting way over."

As Atkinson explained, analytics can estimate what a game's score should have been based on the shots both teams managed to produce and the expected field goal percentage of those shots. Essentially, if both teams shot exactly as the numbers suggest they would over a long sample, this is what the score would be. Atkinson did not specify which games he meant out of the three, but it was likely Game 1, which Cleveland lost in overtime, and Game 3, which New York won, 121-113. Prime Stats has an expected score metric that had Game 3 at a 113-113 tie, and while New York had an expected 10-point win in Game 1, that accounts for overtime. If the actual score had matched what Cleveland's analytics department projected in regulation, the game never would have gotten an extra period and the Cavaliers would have gone up 1-0.

Obviously, despite the expected scores, the Knicks led the series 3-0 at that point and had won those games by 40 total points. They went on to win Game 4 by 37 points, 130-93, though if it's any consolation, the Prime Stats expected score was a slightly less embarrassing 125-100. Both before the Game 4 sweep and afterward, Atkinson's quote was widely mocked. That includes jabs by multiple Knicks, as Josh Hart joked that "I guess we lost analytically" on his podcast with Jalen Brunson, and Karl-Anthony Towns, who said before the ESPYs that "analytically, we should win" the Best Team award. The word "analytically" has become shorthand for anyone attempting to justify an ugly defeat using numbers.

On Saturday, the Cavaliers faced the Knicks for the first time since that series. New York won again, 109-97, and yet again, the expected score was slightly more favorable to Cleveland, with Prime Stats posting an expected score of 112-103. Atkinson did not point to those numbers after Saturday's defeat. Instead, he attempted to explain the widely derided quote, arguing that the quote was taken out of context, which made the soundbite sound less flattering than his actual answer was.

"I would just say there was no coach more complimentary of the Knicks and honest about our performance and how they dominated us," Atkinson told reporters. "So you live and learn a little bit with those things. But like I said, 99% of my comments were how they dominated us. They were by far the better team. I answered the question, as it was taken, [which was] 'And you're down 3-0, what hope do you have of even giving to your guys?'

"We get a lot of information … and I wasn't lying in that sense, but in no sense was it like, 'Oh, man, we deserve to be winning.' Like zero — zero — thought of that."

Atkinson acknowledged that "no one wants to hear" about process when the outcome is a blown 22-point fourth-quarter lead and a 3-0 deficit, but he was trying to figure out how to rally his troops in an impossible situation. His phrasing has become a meme, but when you're down 3-0 in the playoffs, you'll grasp at any signs of positivity you can find. Atkinson had numbers suggesting the two teams were closer than the scoreboard suggested. Using those numbers to try to inspire his team made sense. Putting them out there in public risked exactly the sort of ridicule he ultimately got. The soundbite eclipsed the quote and the context, and the rest is history.

#2600. Ranking NFL's greatest in-season trades of all-time: Where Kirk Cousins to Vikings ranks among top 10

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

While it was quiet for a while, there were plenty of fireworks during the final hours of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline. The biggest trade was the one that sent quarterback Kirk Cousins back to Minnesota.

As it currently stands, that is already one of the most notable in-season trades in NFL history. Quarterbacks of Cousins' stature are almost never traded during a season, especially not to a team that is in position to possibly win a division title. Making this trade even more notable is that the Raiders, who received a third-round pick in exchange for Cousins, will now give the keys to the offense to No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza.

Here's where the Cousins trade already ranks among the biggest in-season deals of all time.

The 1981 Chargers were involved in seismic trades, two of which included receivers. The first sent All-Pro John Jefferson to the Packers in a blockbuster trade that included a 1983 first-round pick and second-round picks in 1982 and 1984.

Two weeks after trading Jefferson, the Chargers traded for then-Saints receiver Wes Chandler, who provided an immediate spark for the "Air Coryell" offense. Chandler helped the Chargers advance to that year's AFC title game. He had 12 catches in two playoff games along with a big punt return for a score in the Chargers' overtime win over the Dolphins in the divisional round.

Chandler led the NFL in receiving yards and touchdown catches the following season and was named to the Pro Bowl three times during his first four seasons in San Diego. Jefferson, however, never again matched the level of success he had with the Chargers.

Wes Chandler 8️⃣9️⃣ pic.twitter.com/bYEvNBFbN9

Tuesday's trade has a chance to be one of the most consequential in NFL history. The trade officially signaled the beginning of the Mendoza era in Las Vegas, and it also infused life into a 6-2 Vikings team that desperately needed help at quarterback.

Tuesday's trade represented a full-circle moment for Cousins, who never wanted to leave Minnesota in the first place. After a two-plus year hiatus, Cousins will get another chance to lead the Vikings on a possible playoff run.

Rams GM Les Snead's "F them picks" philosophy eventually led to a Super Bowl win for the Rams. The trade for Ramsey two years earlier helped make that championship possible.

The Rams gave the Jaguars a first-round selection in the 2020 NFL Draft in addition to first- and fourth- round picks in the 2021 draft for Ramsey, who in 2017 had led the Jaguars within a game of the Super Bowl. Ramsey was named to the Pro Bowl during his first four seasons with the Rams. He had four picks, 16 pass breakups, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery during the Rams' Super Bowl-winning season.

After a 6-10 outfit in 1980, the 49ers were off to a 3-2 start in 1981 when they sent first- and second-round picks in the 1983 NFL Draft to the Chargers in exchange for Dean. Dean was a Pro Bowler each of the previous two years and also mired in a contract dispute.

Just days after coming to San Francisco, Dean had a pair of sacks while helping the 49ers record a 45-14 win over the Cowboys, the same team the 49ers would later defeat in the NFC title game. With the 49ers, Dean recorded 12 sacks in 11 games that season while helping San Francisco win their first Super Bowl. Dean helped San Francisco win another Super Bowl in 1984 before being inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2008.

#49ers greats Randy Cross and Ronnie Lott discuss the legend of Fred Dean. 🚬"James Dean wasn't cooler than Fred Dean."Dean made his #FTTB debut, 43 years ago today — arguably the greatest mid-season acquisition in NFL history.October 11, 1981 pic.twitter.com/jYXDDsTYaK

Bobby Layne was Detroit royalty ... until he wasn't. Five years after leading the Lions to back-to-back NFL titles, Layne was traded to the Steelers just two weeks into the 1958 season. A year earlier, the Lions won their third title with Tobin Rote at quarterback after Layne broke his leg during the second-to-last game of the regular season.

At the time of the trade, Layne allegedly said that the Lions would not win for another 50 years, a statement that became known as the "Bobby Lane Curse." Detroit is still trying to win its first title since 1957.

Layne, who was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1967, played five seasons for the Steelers, earning two Pro Bowls over that span and posting a 27-19-2 record as the team's starting quarterback. He said in his autobiography that his biggest career regret was not winning a title in Pittsburgh.

In Week 5 of the 1983 season, the Raiders suffered their first loss after a 38-37 shootout to Washington, the defending Super Bowl champs who set the NFL single-season scoring record. Al Davis, the Raiders owner and general manager, responded by aggressively pursuing Mike Haynes, who was stuck in a contentious holdout with the Patriots.

While Davis offered Haynes a way out of his situation, Haynes acknowledged decades later that joining the Raiders wasn't an easy decision.

"I actually didn't like the Raiders at all," Haynes told CBS Sports in a 2020 interview. "I didn't like any other team except the Patriots. When Al Davis called, I actually had to think about it. The Raiders were the team where one of my teammates [receiver Darryl Stingley] was paralyzed. I had to think about all that. But I justified it because they had just moved from Oakland to L.A. I grew up in Los Angeles … In my head, I needed to do that to be open to going there. I told Mr. Davis I'd love to go there."

It ended up being a perfect fit for both parties. Haynes teamed up with Lester Hayes to form one of the best cornerback duos in NFL history. The duo shut down Hall of Fame receiver Steve Largent in the AFC title game, and in Super Bowl XVIII, they helped hold Washington's explosive offense to just nine points. The Raiders' 38-9 win remains one of the most surprising outcomes in Super Bowl history.

Haynes played six more seasons with the Raiders, earning three Pro Bowls over that span. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1997. The Patriots, who received a 1984 first-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick, reached the Super Bowl in 1985. Irving Fryer, who was drafted using the 1984 first-round pick, played a key role in the Patriots' first AFC title.

Despite rushing for over 1,000 yards in each of his first two seasons, Lynch was found to be expendable by the Bills midway through the 2010 season. Before the deadline, Buffalo traded Lynch to Seattle in exchange for a 2011 fourth-round pick and a 2012 fifth-round pick.

Simply put, Lynch and the Seahawks were the perfect fit. After running over the defending champion Saints in the 2010 wild card round, Lynch earned Pro Bowl honors in each of his first four full seasons in Seattle.

He was among Seattle's key figures during the team's Super Bowl run in 2013 and NFC Championship run in 2014. In six seasons with the Seahawks, Lynch rushed for 6,347 yards and 79 touchdowns during the regular season, plus 937 yards and nine scores in 11 postseason games.

McCaffrey was dealt to the 49ers in a blockbuster deal that landed the Panthers 2023 second-, third- and fourth-round picks, plus a fifth-rounder in 2024. The trade ended a six-year run in Carolina for McCaffrey, who was selected No. 8 overall in the 2017 NFL Draft.

The deal paid immediate dividends for both McCaffrey and the 49ers, who were 3-3 at the time of the trade. San Francisco reached the NFC title game that year before injuries proved too much to overcome. In 2023, however, the 49ers reached the Super Bowl behind a banner year from McCaffrey, who won his first rushing title that season. San Francisco had the lead in overtime in that year's Super Bowl before falling victim to Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

McCaffrey has remained a highly productive player for the 49ers. This past Sunday, he broke Marshall Faulk's record for the most career touchdown receptions (37) for a running back in the Super Bowl era.

The Rams and Colts stunned the NFL when Indianapolis traded two players, three first-round picks and three second-round picks to Los Angeles in exchange for Dickerson, the league's reigning Offensive Player of the Year. In 1984, he became the first player in NFL history to rush for over 2,100 yards in a season.

Dickerson led the Colts to the playoffs in 1987, their first playoff appearance since the franchise moved from Baltimore to Indianapolis in 1984. The following season, Dickerson led the NFL in rushing, then rushed for over 1,311 yards in 1989.

Happy Halloween #Colts fans! 🎃Here's a look back on this day in 1988 when Eric Dickerson showed up as Superman: pic.twitter.com/zGhWzaQUta

The Rams, despite losing Dickerson, would make the playoffs in each of the next three seasons, which included a trip to the NFC Championship Game in 1989.

The Buffalo Bills were also part of this trade, giving up several assets that included future high picks in exchange for future All-Pro linebacker Cornelius Bennett, who would help the Bills become the first team in NFL history to appear in four consecutive Super Bowls during the 1990s.

"I find out that we had just traded the only guy on our team that was really any good. And I couldn't believe it."

Troy Aikman, needless to say, wasn't thrilled upon hearing the news that the Dallas Cowboys and new head coach Jimmy Johnson had traded their best player, running back Herschel Walker, to the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for a bounty of future draft picks. Walker, a former Heisman Trophy winner and 1,500-yard back the previous season, was leaving a team that would ultimately go 1-15 during Johnson's first season in Dallas. While the trade was widely unpopular at the time, Johnson was confident that it was the right thing to do.

"One agent said it's the biggest trade he has ever seen in the NFL," Johnson said during a press conference following the trade, "and one owner said it's a great train robbery. Whatever it is, we're happy with it."

The Cowboys used the picks to help build what would become one of the best rosters in NFL history. In 1990, they used their first pick from the trade to select Emmitt Smith, who would go on to become the NFL's all-time leading rusher. Over the following two drafts, the Cowboys selected future Pro Bowl defensive tackle Russell Maryland, perennial starting cornerback Kevin Smith, and future three-time All-Pro safety Darren Woodson.

A blockbuster trade that sparked the beginning of a dynasty.29 years ago today, the Vikings acquired RB Herschel Walker... And the rest is history for the @dallascowboys. #TDIH #FBF (via @nflthrowback) pic.twitter.com/UG8gHsgehr

Along with several other acquisitions, the Cowboys went from NFL doormats to NFL champions. In 1992, just three years after pulling off the greatest deadline deal in league history, Dallas won the first of its three Super Bowls over four years.

"I couldn't understand it at the time, but I'm glad they viewed it differently," Aikman said during an interview with NFL Films. "It certainly got us over the hump in a hurry."

#2597. FIGC, Galliani e Malagò davanti al TFN: voto del 14 dicembre a rischio

La Federazione si costituisce nel procedimento sulla commissione incaricata di controllare le candidature.

La FIGC ha deciso di costituirsi davanti al Tribunale Federale Nazionale nel procedimento avviato dal ricorso di Adriano Galliani contro la commissione nominata da Giovanni Malagò per verificare le candidature alla presidenza federale. Secondo quanto riportato da Onefootball, Il TFN ascolterà le parti prima di pronunciarsi collegialmente. La controversia potrebbe far slittare le elezioni, per ora fissate al 14 dicembre.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Secondo Onefootball, il calendario della procedura è già stretto: l’elenco dei candidati ammessi dovrebbe essere pubblicato entro il 14 novembre. Il limite stabilito dal CONI per celebrare l’assemblea elettiva resta il 31 gennaio 2027.

Galliani ha presentato il ricorso lunedì 9 novembre tramite il proprio legale, l’avvocato Filippo Lattanzi. L’atto riguarda la commissione istituita il 2 novembre da Malagò, commissario straordinario della FIGC e a sua volta candidato alla presidenza. All’organismo è stato affidato il controllo della regolarità delle candidature.

Per Galliani, la commissione non sarebbe prevista dalle norme statutarie e regolamentari della Federazione e non avrebbe quindi titolo per effettuare quelle verifiche. Il ricorso contesta anche la scelta di istituirla da parte di Malagò, direttamente coinvolto nella competizione elettorale.

La richiesta al TFN è di sospendere in via cautelare l’efficacia del provvedimento e poi annullarlo. Secondo la posizione sostenuta da Galliani, il controllo delle candidature dovrebbe essere svolto dagli organi già individuati dalle norme federali, in particolare dalla Segreteria generale e dal segretario Marco Brunelli. Galliani è sostenuto da Assocalciatori e Assoallenatori.

Nel confronto sulle candidature ha un peso anche la posizione del Genoa. In un primo momento l’amministratore delegato rossoblù Andres Blazquez aveva sottoscritto l’accredito a favore di Galliani. Successivamente il presidente Dan Sucu ha espresso il sostegno del club a Malagò, accompagnandolo con una comunicazione formale di revoca e diffida relativa alla precedente adesione.

Malagò ha presentato undici accrediti di club di Serie A, esattamente il minimo richiesto. Se quello del Genoa non fosse considerato valido, uno degli undici sostegni necessari verrebbe meno e la candidatura potrebbe non soddisfare il requisito previsto.

Il ricorso di Galliani, però, non chiede direttamente l’esclusione di Malagò. Il suo oggetto principale è la legittimità della commissione incaricata dei controlli. La posizione del Genoa resta un elemento del contenzioso e potrebbe assumere rilievo nella successiva valutazione dei requisiti.

#2596. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

#2595. Thunder trade grades: OKC swipes promising young wing Nique Clifford from the rebuilding Kings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We have our first trade of the 2026-27 NBA season, and it's a somewhat familiar one. The Oklahoma City Thunder are acquiring guard Nique Clifford from the Sacramento Kings, according to ESPN, reversing a trade that occurred during the 2025 NBA Draft. The Thunder, using a pick acquired from the Los Angeles Clippers, were on the clock at No. 24 overall, but the Kings moved into that slot to select Clifford. Now, a bit more than a year later, Clifford lands with the team whose hat he wore on draft night.

Trades this early in an NBA season are rare. Until Dec. 15, around 29% of the league is still technically untradeable because of contracts signed over the summer. However, the Oklahoma City Thunder have been ravaged by injuries so far this season. They initially planned to use their open roster spot to sign former first-round pick Ochai Agbaji, but changed course before doing so as their health issues worsened. Instead, they signed Dalen Terry to a non-guaranteed deal; they will now presumably waive him in order to take a swing on Sacramento's promising youngster. With the season's first trade done, let's grade it for both sides.

One of the advantages of working with the enormous draft surplus Oklahoma City has had since it traded Paul George to the Clippers is that it allows the Thunder to be opportunistic. Think of last February, when they stole Jared McCain from the Philadelphia 76ers for a single first-round pick. McCain was struggling through such a tough year that few teams could have afforded the risk of giving up a first-rounder for him. The Thunder obviously could, and in doing so, they got a key performer with two and a half years of cheap cost control remaining.

The thinking here is somewhat similar. The Thunder have so many second-round picks that they wouldn't miss two of them. The Kings, like the 76ers, decided they were ready to cut bait on a recent first-round pick who had shown promise far earlier than most teams would have, so the Thunder, with access to a roster spot through Terry's non-guaranteed deal and second-round picks to spare, jumped at the chance to take a swing on yet another valuable asset with several years of cost control.

Is Clifford going to be as helpful for Oklahoma City as McCain? Probably not, but there's plenty of reason to believe he can help this depleted version of the Thunder. Clifford averaged just under 13 points, five rebounds and four assists in March and April last year for a Kings team that may have been terrible, but wasn't actively trying to lose like many of its contemporaries.

His emergence as a genuine NBA Draft prospect came in his last two collegiate seasons, when he improved as a 3-point shooter playing at Colorado State. That shooting, coupled with his all-around production and bothersome 6-foot-8 wingspan as a defender, made him a promising role player prospect. Clifford does a little bit of everything. If the shots are falling, pretty much anyone could use a high-IQ, high-motor, ball-handling wing who rebounds well for his position.

This is, again, a flyer. We might find out that the Kings are giving up on him because they think he's a lemon. Think of their decision to dump Devin Carter two years after picking him in the lottery. Sometimes teams just know. Of course, the Kings are hardly the best evaluators of their own talent. See: Haliburton, Tyrese. We can't give the Thunder a straight "A" here because we've only ever seen Clifford as a productive player at the end of a single regular season for a terrible team. For all we know, the end of last season was a March mirage for Clifford. Plenty of teams fall for those.

But the cost here, for Oklahoma City's purposes, effectively amounts to loose change it found between its couch cushions. The upside is a real rotation player it can afford for several years. That's the definition of "low risk, high reward.

When the Kings drafted Clifford, he was joining a version of the team that still harbored (admittedly delusional) visions of remaining competitive. After last season, the plan changed. The Kings are moving into a rebuild now, and everything Sacramento does is geared toward the development of No. 7 overall pick Darius Acuff Jr., who currently has the second-highest rookie usage rate in NBA history. After averaging 25 minutes per game last season, Clifford has played just 50 through eight games this season. He hasn't made his shots in that small sample, which is a critical trait for anyone attempting to play off of Acuff.

Now, we're in the post-tanking NBA. In the past, we could have more fully admonished the Kings for playing veterans who won't be a part of their future, like Zach LaVine and Malik Monk, while plastering Clifford to the bench. Sacramento wants to avoid the relegation zone, so that makes a bit more sense now than it might have in the past. Couple that with the emergence of second-round pick Emanuel Sharp and former undrafted free agent Leaky Black as parts of the rotation and the impending return of Keegan Murray from a sprained ankle, and suddenly there just weren't many perimeter minutes available in Sacramento.

That all sounds fine on paper, but the NBA isn't a paper league. Players get hurt. Players get traded. Circumstances change. This was not something that needed to get settled in November of Clifford's second season. Even the Sixers waited until February to move McCain a season ago. Inevitably, there would have been more opportunities for the Kings to see what they had in Clifford as part of the Acuff-centric version of the team had they simply waited for those opportunities to arise. Sacramento simply has not earned the benefit of the doubt a team would need to justify giving up on a young player who has shown actual promise this quickly.

If this was a financially driven decision, it was still a hasty one. The Kings still had a year before they needed to make a decision on his fourth-year option. They already dropped below the luxury tax by waiving and stretching DeMar DeRozan, and there is not an immediately apparent benefit to saving another $3.3 million or so underneath it. Perhaps one will present itself later, but moving a player at this price point is typically easy enough that the Kings didn't have to rush this.

If this is a low-risk, high-reward trade for the Thunder, it's the opposite for the Kings. Best-case scenario, they're right about Clifford's value... and they get two second-round picks for someone they themselves decided was worth trading up to No. 24 to get. Not a great look for the organization. If they're wrong about Clifford and the Thunder manage to turn him into a real player as they do for almost everyone they acquire, they not only lose out on a valuable, cost-controlled asset, but become an object of ridicule for what feels like the hundredth time in the past two decades.

Last year's NBA Finals was a battle between Sacramento's former point guard (De'Aaron Fox and the San Antonio Spurs) and its former coach (Mike Brown and the New York Knicks). The 2025 Finals were nearly won by Haliburton, another former Kings point guard, and the 2023 Finals were won by Michael Malone, another former Kings coach. It's obviously unlikely that the Thunder manage to rally past all of these injuries and make it back to the Finals, and it's probably less likely that Clifford is the single reason why that would happen, but if he turns out to be a real part of a resurgent Thunder team, that will mark yet another humiliation for this Kings organization.

There's only one way to describe last week in the NFL: Chalk.

Favorites dominated the Week 9 slate as just one upset occurred while every other favorite took care of business. That was music to our ears because we saw the week playing out that exact way, dialing up a perfect 15-0 record on the moneyline. The only underdog we liked last week was Green Bay, and they proved us right as they rolled into Foxborough and steamrolled the Patriots. That not only helped me notch a pristine moneyline record but also cashed one of my five Locks of the Week.

There, I was 3-2 ATS, which jived with my more modest 8-7 ATS record for the week overall. That's not as stellar as the straight-up mark, but we were above .500, so we made money. And that's what we're after at the end of the day.

I'll try to keep the momentum rolling into Week 10 where, unlike last week, I do have a fair share of underdogs pulling off the upsets. That includes the Pittsburgh Steelers, who land inside my five Locks of the Week.

Note: Chicago, Denver, Philadelphia, and Tampa Bay are on the bye in Week 10.

There's arguably no offense hotter right now than the Bengals. Over their four-game winning streak, they've averaged over 35 points per game, and Joe Burrow has been playing at an MVP level. The Cincinnati QB has 18 total touchdowns over this stretch and a 132.0 passer rating. Simply put, they've been a bulldozer. However, I do think it's worth pointing out who they've played over the course of the winning streak: at Dolphins, at Ravens (no Lamar Jackson), vs. Titans and vs. Falcons. Not exactly a murderer's row.

Pittsburgh, who beat these Bengals back in Week 3, should provide much more resistance than what they've faced recently. The Steelers defense is tied for the fifth-lowest yards per play average (5.0), tied for the fourth-lowest points per game allowed (18.0), and tied for the eighth-lowest passer rating allowed (83.3). Meanwhile, Cincinnati's defense is tied for the most yards per rush attempt allowed so far this season (5.0), which sets up Jaylen Warren to continue his ascent as one of the true breakout players of the season.

On top of this being a potential mismatch for the Bengals going up against this stout Steelers team, their scheduling surrounding this game does them no favors either. While they'll be at home in Week 10, Cincinnati is coming off an international game in Madrid last week. As for the Steelers, they're fresh off their bye week, creating a sizable rest discrepancy. All of this is a recipe for an upset.

Projected score: Steelers 27, Bengals 24The pick: Steelers +3.5

Bryce Young doesn't have the best history going up against the Saints, as the Panthers quarterback is just 1-5 against his division foe in his career. That said, I think there's a window here for him to get a rare victory against New Orleans on Sunday.

While his numbers have come down since his stellar start to begin the season, Young started to look more like himself in the loss to Denver, completing 71.7% of his passes to go along with three touchdowns. The Saints secondary is allowing 7.3 yards per attempt so far this season, which is tied for the fifth-highest in the league. Their 99.5 passer rating allowed is also the seventh-highest in the NFL. This isn't as daunting a matchup for Young, who had to face Tampa Bay, Green Bay, and Denver over Carolina's recent three-game losing streak. I like him to rebound here.

Meanwhile, New Orleans is 1-4 straight-up and 0-5 ATS at home this season, so the Superdome hasn't been too friendly thus far.

Projected score: Panthers 24, Saints 21The pick: Panthers +1.5

Similar to what we discussed with Cincinnati, the Falcons do have to deal with immediately playing the following week after an international game in Madrid last Sunday. That may only put them further behind the eight ball against a Chiefs team that cruised to a 35-12 win over the Jets last week. Patrick Mahomes did give us all a scare in the midst of that game after injuring his elbow, but it doesn't appear serious enough to keep him out of this matchup.

Mahomes has thrown five touchdowns and no interceptions over his past two games, but his lack of a downfield threat has been noticeable. He's averaging an NFL-low 5.6 air yards per attempt this season as the Chiefs have really looked for pass catches to put up yards after the catch. Well, they just acquired some help in that regard in Josh Downs, whom they brought in before the deadline in a trade with the Colts. The wideout has a knack for creating separation and now has a capable quarterback to deliver the football to him, so Kansas City could see quick dividends from this addition. That's especially true against a Falcons secondary that was just lit up by the Bengals last week and just traded away star safety Jessie Bates III to the Jaguars.

#2593. Jayson Tatum won't give air to Jaylen Brown drama ahead of Celtics-Sixers game: 'Another game on the schedule'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- Jayson Tatum downplayed Tuesday's showdown between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which will be the first time that he and former teammate Jaylen Brown will face each other as opponents.

"It's another game on the schedule. It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one," Tatum said after putting up 21 points, four rebounds and six assists in a 117-97 win over the Milwaukee Bucks. "This one counted as one. Go get ready for Tuesday. It's a really good team, obviously. Incredible group, great coaching staff, they've been playing really well. So from that standpoint it's gonna be fun. But it's nothing more than Celtics versus Sixers."

Tatum and Brown spent nine seasons together, and led the Celtics to the 2024 championship -- the historic franchise's first since 2008 and record-setting 18th overall -- before the latter was traded to Philadelphia this summer in a blockbuster deal that brought Paul George to Boston.

Much has been made about Tatum and Brown's relationship, or lack thereof, particularly over the last few weeks.

Late last month, Tatum shared his recollection of the trade in an episode of his documentary series, "Summer of Jayson." "I was just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world," he said. In the comment section of the clip online, Brown called "cap."

Shortly after, Tatum tried to shut down any drama by pointing to all that they had accomplished together. "This ain't no f---in' Shaq and Kobe, there's no beef," Tatum said. "It's not about that. It should be more praise, and I understand that don't necessarily sell. Drama gets clicks and views, but I'm not really — that's not my thing."

Brown, on the other hand, played into the drama a few days later. "There's no beef," Brown said. "Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. It's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chop. And some gravy. He should stay ready at all times."

Now, as the first meeting between the former teammates arrives, both have tried to keep the focus on basketball.

"It's nothing to talk about. I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said after the 76ers secured a 127-121 win over the Chicago Bulls on Sunday. "Just playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win, so it's nothing to talk about. Just check the ball up. ... "We'll see how I feel when we get out there, but as of now, I got no emotion towards anything. So I'm just ready to go."

When Tatum asked if he would have a conversation with Brown on Tuesday, his response was a simple "I'm not able to tell the future," before adding that he had "no idea" if any such conversation would have to wait until after the season.

"I just know that it's the Celtics versus the Sixers. Just go out there and do my job and try to get another win," Tatum said. "Get through that, got a game on Wednesday. It's a long season. We got 72 games left. That's just the focus right now."

As for the actual basketball, both players and teams are off to terrific starts. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists on 47.7% shooting, including 39.2% from 3-point range, for the 9-2 Sixers, who sit atop the Eastern Conference. Tatum, meanwhile, is at 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists for the 8-2 Celtics, who are alone in second.

#2592. Fernando Mendoza new favorite to win Offensive Rookie of the Year ahead of his first NFL start

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Minnesota Vikings beat the buzzer at Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, as they sent the Las Vegas Raiders a third-round pick for quarterback Kirk Cousins. There were plenty of winners in this trade.

The Vikings get better at the most important position in football, the Raiders got nice compensation, and Cousins upgrades his own situation — going from 4-5 to 6-2 with Justin Jefferson. And then, there's Fernando Mendoza.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft is now the Raiders' new starter, and because he's been promoted to first-string, Mendoza is now your new favorite to win Offensive Rookie of the Year over at DraftKings Sportsbook.

It's pretty shocking to see a player making his first career start in Week 10 be favored to win Offensive Rookie of the Year, but that just spotlights the fact that no one else in the class has really been able to separate.

Boston and Concepcion in Cleveland are the first teammate duo to rank 1-2 in rookie receiving yards through Week 9 in NFL history, but neither are inside the top 20 of receiving when it comes to the entire league. Coleman appears to be the new RB1 in Denver, but he hasn't crossed 60 yards rushing in a single game this season. Then there's Tate in Tennessee, who had a nine-catch, 145-yard explosion against the Baltimore Ravens last month, but his production has been inconsistent.

It's possible one of those players steps up and ends the regular season on a tear, but the door is open for Mendoza to win rookie of the year despite the fact that he's completed just 6 of 8 passes for 48 yards halfway through the season.

"This is something that he's worked very hard for since the moment he's walked into this building," Raiders general manager John Spytek said of Mendoza. "He passed every test. ... He put us in a position where we had to make a very hard decision today with his growth as a person, as a teammate, as a leader, as a quarterback."

Mendoza has to be ready to roll immediately, because the Raiders have a few tough defenses coming up on their schedule. Mendoza will become the first No. 1 overall pick quarterback in NFL history to make his first career start against the defending Super Bowl champions, per CBS Sports Research, as Vegas hosts the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday. Mendoza also becomes the first No. 1 overall pick quarterback to make his first career start against the NFL's No. 1 defense since Vinny Testaverde in 1987.

In Week 11, Mendoza makes his first road start against the Broncos, who rank top five in sacks and are currently on a five-game win streak. In Week 12 come the Browns, who have gone 54 straight games without allowing a 300-yard passer. That's tied for the longest streak in the NFL over the past 40 seasons.

Still, the Raiders feel as though the rookie is prepared for the moment. Sportsbooks seem to think so, too.

"He's prepared," Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak said. "He practices extremely well, and his work habits also allowed us to make this trade because we feel that he's ready to go. And we're excited for him to take the ball for the game here this Sunday."
